lessons.title: What an Algorithm Is
lessons.content:
Imagine your mother asks you to make cha for six guests. You boil water, add tea leaves, add milk and sugar, let it simmer, then pour it into six cups. You did not think about it much, but you just followed an algorithm. An algorithm is simply a clear list of steps that takes some starting things and turns them into the result you want. This whole course is about two big questions: how do we design good step lists, and how do we measure how good they are?

The official definition: An algorithm is a finite sequence of well-defined instructions that takes some input, does some work, and produces an output that solves a given problem. The word comes from the name of the Persian mathematician Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, who wrote about step-by-step methods for arithmetic more than a thousand years ago. When Europeans translated his books, his name turned into "algorismus", and later "algorithm".

Problem versus instance: A problem is the general question, like "sort a list of numbers into increasing order". An instance is one specific input, like the list 7, 3, 9, 1. An algorithm must work for every instance of the problem, not just the one you tried on paper. That is a big difference from simply solving a puzzle once. If your sorting method works for 7, 3, 9, 1 but breaks when two numbers are equal, it is not a correct sorting algorithm.

The five properties: Most textbooks, including the ones used at BUET, DU and KUET, list five properties every algorithm must have. Input: it takes zero or more inputs. Output: it produces at least one output. Definiteness: every step is precise and has only one meaning, so "add a little salt" is not definite, but "add 5 grams of salt" is. Finiteness: it must stop after a finite number of steps for every input. Effectiveness: every step is basic enough that it could be done exactly, in a finite amount of time, even with pencil and paper.

Why finiteness matters: Look at this tiny method: "start at 1, keep adding 2 until you reach 10". You get 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 and so on, and you never hit exactly 10. It runs forever. That is not an algorithm, it is a bug. A real algorithm needs a stopping rule that is guaranteed to be reached, like "stop when the number is bigger than 10".

Algorithm versus program: An algorithm is the idea. A program is that idea written in a particular language like C, Java or Python, for a particular computer. The same algorithm, say binary search, can be written as a program in ten different languages. In this course we usually write algorithms in pseudocode, which is like simple English mixed with code, so we can focus on the idea and not on semicolons.

A first example, finding the maximum: Problem: given n numbers, find the largest. Algorithm: set best = A[1]; for i = 2 to n, if A[i] > best then best = A[i]; return best. Try it on 4, 9, 2, 7. best starts at 4, becomes 9 at the second number, stays 9 for 2 and 7. Output 9. It takes exactly n - 1 comparisons. Can any algorithm do better? No: every number except the winner must lose at least one comparison, so at least n - 1 comparisons are needed. This kind of thinking, "what is the least work any method must do", is called a lower bound, and we will see it again for sorting.

Correctness: The first thing we ask about any algorithm is "does it always give the right answer?" Testing a few inputs is not enough, because the one input you did not test might break it. So we prove correctness. For loops, the main tool is a loop invariant: a statement that is true before the loop starts, stays true after each round, and at the end gives us what we want. For the maximum algorithm, the invariant is "best is the largest of A[1..i-1]". It is true at the start (i = 2, best = A[1]), each round keeps it true, and when the loop ends, best is the largest of the whole array. Lesson 3 goes deeper into this.

Efficiency: The second question is "how much resource does it use?" The two main resources are time (how many steps) and space (how much extra memory). We do not measure time in seconds, because seconds depend on the computer, the language, and even what else is running. Instead we count basic steps as a function of the input size n. For finding the maximum, the step count is about n. For checking every pair of numbers it is about n squared divided by 2.

The RAM model: To count steps fairly, we pretend the computer is a simple machine called the Random Access Machine. In this model, each simple operation, like adding two numbers, comparing, assigning a value, or reading A[i], takes one unit of time. Memory access to any cell costs the same. There is one processor doing one thing at a time. Real computers have caches and parallel cores, but this simple model predicts how algorithms grow surprisingly well.

Why speed really matters: Suppose you have 1 million numbers. An algorithm that takes about n squared steps needs about 10 to the power 12 steps, a trillion. A computer doing a billion simple steps a second would need about 1000 seconds, over 16 minutes. An algorithm that takes about n log n steps needs about 20 million steps, finished in a fiftieth of a second. Buying a computer 10 times faster helps the slow one a little; picking the better algorithm helps a million times more. That is why companies care so much about algorithms.

Input size: We always describe cost in terms of the input size n. For a list, n is the number of items. For a graph, we use two numbers: V, the number of vertices, and E, the number of edges. For a number like in primality testing, the size is the number of digits or bits, not the value itself. This last point surprises many students and becomes important near the end of the course.

Best, worst and average case: For the same n, different inputs can take different time. Linear search for a value in a list of n items finishes after 1 check if the item is first (best case) but needs n checks if it is last or missing (worst case). We usually care most about the worst case, because it is a guarantee: the algorithm will never be slower than this. The average case needs an assumption about what inputs look like.

Design paradigms, the tools in your toolbox: Most of this course is about general strategies for designing algorithms. Brute force tries everything. Divide and conquer breaks a problem into smaller copies, solves them, and combines the answers, like merge sort. Greedy makes the choice that looks best right now and never goes back, like giving change with the biggest note first. Dynamic programming solves small subproblems once, saves the answers in a table and builds up bigger answers. Backtracking explores choices and steps back as soon as a choice cannot work, like solving a maze. Each paradigm fits some problems and fails on others, and a big skill is knowing which one to try.

The course map: First, we build the measuring tools: asymptotic notation, counting loops and solving recurrences. Then divide and conquer with merge sort, quick sort and friends, plus why comparison sorting cannot beat n log n. Next come selection and amortized analysis. Then greedy algorithms and dynamic programming, the two big design ideas. Then graph algorithms: searching, spanning trees, shortest paths and maximum flow. Then backtracking and string matching. Finally the famous question of P versus NP, and what to do when a problem is too hard to solve exactly.

Real-life example 1, Pathao route: When you book a Pathao ride from Mirpur to Motijheel, the app must suggest a route. Dhaka's roads can be seen as a graph: intersections are points, roads are lines, and each line has a travel time. Trying every possible route would take forever because the number of routes explodes. Instead, apps use shortest-path algorithms like Dijkstra's (lesson 20), which cleverly grow the set of places whose best time is known, one at a time. The result comes back in a fraction of a second.

Real-life example 2, exam result sorting: Imagine the education board must sort the scores of about 1.5 million SSC candidates to make merit lists. With an n squared method like bubble sort, that is around 2 times 10 to the power 12 comparisons, slow even on a server. With merge sort it is about n log2 n, around 1.5 million times 21, roughly 31 million comparisons, which takes well under a second. Same computer, same data, a totally different experience.

How to describe an algorithm: There are four common ways. Plain English steps are easy to read but can be unclear. A flowchart uses boxes and arrows and is good for beginners. Pseudocode is the standard in this course, because it is precise but not tied to any language. Finally, real code in C, C++, Java or Python is what you actually run. In exams, clear pseudocode with good indentation is usually what teachers want.

Space matters too: Besides time, we measure extra memory. Finding the maximum needs only one extra variable, best, no matter how big n is, so its extra space is constant. Merge sort, which you will meet in lesson 6, needs an extra array of size n while merging. Sometimes we trade one for the other: storing more answers in memory can save a lot of time, which is exactly the idea behind dynamic programming. On a phone with little RAM or a tiny microcontroller, space can matter even more than time.

Common mistakes: Students often think an algorithm is "correct" because it worked on the example from class. Always think about edge cases: an empty list, one item, all items equal, negative numbers, already sorted input. Another mistake is measuring speed in seconds on your own laptop and comparing it with a friend's laptop. Count steps instead. A third mistake is mixing up the problem with the algorithm: sorting is a problem, merge sort is one algorithm for it.

What exams ask: Typical questions include: define an algorithm and state its properties; explain the difference between an algorithm and a program; write an algorithm to find the maximum or the sum of n numbers and count its steps; explain why we use step counts instead of seconds; and define best, worst and average case with an example such as linear search.

Recap: An algorithm is a finite, precise, effective list of steps that turns input into correct output for every instance of a problem. We judge it by correctness first and efficiency second, counting steps in the simple RAM model as a function of input size n. The rest of the course gives you better measuring tools and a toolbox of design paradigms, so that you can pick or invent the fast recipe and not the slow one.
key_points: An algorithm is a finite sequence of precise steps that solves every instance of a problem.
Five properties: input, output, definiteness, finiteness, effectiveness.
An algorithm is the idea; a program is the idea written in a specific language.
Correctness is proved, often with loop invariants, not just tested on a few inputs.
Efficiency is measured by counting basic steps as a function of input size n in the RAM model.
Worst case gives a guarantee; best and average cases describe other inputs.
Main design paradigms: brute force, divide and conquer, greedy, dynamic programming, backtracking.
lessons.tip: For every algorithm you meet in this course, ask two questions out loud: why is it correct, and how many steps does it take? If you can answer both, you really understand it.
lessons.task: Write pseudocode on paper that finds both the smallest and the largest of 8 numbers. Run it by hand on 5, 12, 3, 8, 19, 1, 7, 10 and count how many comparisons you made.

quiz.q: Which property says an algorithm must stop after a finite number of steps?
quiz.explain: Finiteness means the algorithm always terminates.

quiz.q: Why do we count steps instead of measuring seconds?
options: Step counts do not depend on the machine or language
quiz.explain: Seconds change with hardware and software; step counts describe the algorithm itself.

quiz.q: How many comparisons does the simple find-maximum algorithm make on n numbers?
quiz.explain: It compares each of the remaining n - 1 numbers with the current best once.

quiz.q: In linear search, when does the worst case happen?
options: The item is last or not present
quiz.explain: Then every one of the n items must be checked.

quiz.q: Which paradigm saves answers of small subproblems in a table to build bigger answers?
quiz.explain: Dynamic programming stores subproblem answers so each is solved only once.

lessons.title: Asymptotic Notation: Big-O, Omega and Theta
lessons.content:
Think about two rickshaw pullers racing from Farmgate to Shahbag. One is faster at the start, the other has a better rhythm. Over 100 metres the first one might win. Over 10 kilometres, the steady one wins easily. Algorithms are the same. For small inputs, almost anything is fast. What really matters is how the running time grows when the input gets huge. Asymptotic notation is the language we use to talk about that growth, while ignoring small details that do not matter in the long run.

Why we throw away details: Suppose one algorithm takes 3n^2 + 5n + 2 steps. When n = 1000, the 3n^2 part is 3,000,000, the 5n part is only 5,000, and the 2 is nothing. As n grows, the biggest term completely dominates. Also, the constant 3 depends on the machine and how carefully we count. So we simply say the algorithm grows like n^2. That is the heart of asymptotic analysis: keep the dominant term, drop lower terms and constant factors.

Big-O, the upper bound: We write f(n) = O(g(n)) if there exist positive constants c and n0 such that 0 <= f(n) <= c times g(n) for all n >= n0. In plain words: after some point n0, f never grows faster than a constant multiple of g. Big-O is like saying "at most". It is an upper bound on growth.

Proving a Big-O bound, worked example: Show that f(n) = 3n^2 + 5n + 2 is O(n^2). For n >= 1, we know n <= n^2 and 1 <= n^2. So 3n^2 + 5n + 2 <= 3n^2 + 5n^2 + 2n^2 = 10n^2. Choose c = 10 and n0 = 1, and the definition is satisfied. Notice we do not need the smallest possible c; any c that works is fine. That freedom makes these proofs quite easy once you see the trick of replacing every term by the biggest one.

Big-Omega, the lower bound: We write f(n) = Omega(g(n)) if there exist positive constants c and n0 such that 0 <= c times g(n) <= f(n) for all n >= n0. Omega is like "at least". For our example, 3n^2 + 5n + 2 >= 3n^2 for all n >= 1, so with c = 3 and n0 = 1, f(n) = Omega(n^2). Omega is used for lower bounds such as "any comparison sort needs Omega(n log n) comparisons".

Big-Theta, the tight bound: We write f(n) = Theta(g(n)) if there are positive constants c1, c2 and n0 such that c1 g(n) <= f(n) <= c2 g(n) for all n >= n0. Theta means "grows exactly like, up to constants". A function is Theta(g) exactly when it is both O(g) and Omega(g). For our example we showed 3n^2 <= f(n) <= 10n^2 for n >= 1, so f(n) = Theta(n^2) with c1 = 3, c2 = 10, n0 = 1.

An analogy with comparisons: It helps to think of O as "less than or equal", Omega as "greater than or equal", and Theta as "equal", all about growth rates and not about exact values. So n = O(n^2) is true, just like 3 <= 5 is true, even though it is not tight. Many students write O when they mean Theta. In daily speech programmers say "binary search is O(log n)" and usually mean Theta, but in exams be precise.

Showing a bound is false: Is n^2 = O(n)? Suppose it were. Then there would be c and n0 with n^2 <= c n for all n >= n0. Divide by n: n <= c for all large n. But n keeps growing and eventually passes any fixed c, for example at n = c + 1. Contradiction, so n^2 is not O(n). The pattern of such proofs is always: assume the constants exist, then find a large n that breaks the inequality.

Little-o and little-omega: Sometimes we want a strict bound. f(n) = o(g(n)) means f grows strictly slower than g: for every positive constant c, there is an n0 such that f(n) < c g(n) for all n >= n0. For example 2n = o(n^2), but 2n^2 is not o(n^2). Similarly f(n) = omega(g(n)) means f grows strictly faster, like n^2 = omega(n). Think of little-o as "strictly less" and little-omega as "strictly greater".

The limit trick: An easy way to compare two functions is to look at the limit of f(n) divided by g(n) as n goes to infinity. If the limit is 0, then f = o(g), so also f = O(g). If the limit is a positive finite constant, then f = Theta(g). If the limit is infinity, then f = omega(g), so also f = Omega(g). Example: f = n log n and g = n^2. The ratio is log n divided by n, which goes to 0, so n log n = o(n^2). When the limit is hard, L'Hopital's rule from calculus often helps.

The growth-rate ladder: Here are the common functions from slowest to fastest: 1 (constant), log n, square root of n, n, n log n, n^2, n^3, 2^n, n!, and n^n. Every step up the ladder is a different world. At n = 1000, log2 n is about 10, n log n about 10,000, n^2 a million, n^3 a billion, and 2^n has more than 300 digits. Polynomial functions like n^2 and n^3 are considered manageable; exponential ones like 2^n become impossible very quickly.

Logs and their bases: Students often ask whether log base 2 or log base 10 matters. In asymptotic notation it does not. Because log_a n = log_b n divided by log_b a, two logs with different bases differ only by a constant factor, and constants disappear. So we just write O(log n). But exponents are different: 2^n and 4^n are not Theta of each other, because 4^n = 2^n times 2^n, and the extra factor 2^n is not a constant.

Some handy rules: First, constant factors vanish: 100n is Theta(n). Second, the sum rule: O(f) + O(g) = O(max(f, g)), so doing an O(n) step and then an O(n^2) step costs O(n^2) overall. Third, the product rule: if a loop runs O(f) times and each run costs O(g), the total is O(f times g). Fourth, any polynomial of degree d with a positive leading coefficient is Theta(n^d). Fifth, any power of log n grows slower than any power of n, so (log n)^3 = o(square root of n).

Properties: The notations behave like inequalities. They are transitive: if f = O(g) and g = O(h), then f = O(h). They are reflexive: f = Theta(f). Theta is symmetric: f = Theta(g) exactly when g = Theta(f). And there is transpose symmetry: f = O(g) exactly when g = Omega(f). These properties let you chain bounds together in proofs.

Tricky exam examples: Is 2^(n+1) = O(2^n)? Yes, because 2^(n+1) = 2 times 2^n, a constant factor. Is 2^(2n) = O(2^n)? No, because 2^(2n) = 4^n, which is 2^n times 2^n. Is log(n!) = Theta(n log n)? Yes. A quick reason: n! is at most n^n, so log(n!) <= n log n; and n! is at least (n/2)^(n/2), because the larger half of the factors are each at least n/2, so log(n!) >= (n/2) log(n/2), which is Omega(n log n).

O is not the same as worst case: This is a very common confusion. Best case, worst case and average case are about which input we look at. O, Omega and Theta are about how a function grows. You can say "the worst-case time of insertion sort is Theta(n^2)" and also "the best-case time of insertion sort is Theta(n)". Each case is a function of n, and each function can be described with any of the notations.

Real-life example 1, mobile data plan: A Grameenphone or Robi data pack costs a fixed fee plus nothing extra per MB, while a pay-as-you-go plan costs money per MB. For tiny usage, pay-as-you-go may be cheaper. But as your usage grows, the pay-per-MB cost grows like n while the pack stays constant. Asymptotically the pack is O(1) and pay-as-you-go is Theta(n), and for heavy users the constant one wins. Asymptotic thinking is about "who wins when things get big".

Real-life example 2, inviting guests to a wedding: Suppose you must send each guest a card. That is Theta(n) work for n guests. Now suppose every guest must shake hands with every other guest. That is n(n - 1)/2 handshakes, which is Theta(n^2). For 20 guests that is 190 handshakes, fine. For a 1000-guest Bangladeshi wedding it is 499,500 handshakes, which would take days. The jump from n to n^2 is exactly what notation helps you spot before you start.

How big can n be? A useful rule of thumb from programming contests: a normal computer does roughly 10^8 to 10^9 simple steps per second. So within about one second, a Theta(n) algorithm can handle n of tens of millions, Theta(n log n) can handle a few million, Theta(n^2) a few thousand to about ten thousand, Theta(n^3) a few hundred, and Theta(2^n) only about 25 to 30. When a problem says n is up to 100,000, that alone tells you an n^2 method is too slow and you need something like n log n. This is asymptotic notation used as a planning tool.

A worked ordering example: Arrange these by growth: n^2, 2^(log2 n), n log n, 100, square root of n, n!, 3^n. First simplify: 2^(log2 n) is just n. Then the order is 100, square root of n, n, n log n, n^2, 3^n, n!. The last two need care: 3^n grows fast, but n! eventually beats any c^n, because n! multiplies by bigger and bigger numbers each step while 3^n always multiplies by 3.

Common mistakes: Writing O(2n) or O(n^2 + n) instead of O(n) and O(n^2); always simplify. Forgetting that the definition only needs to hold for n >= n0, not for every n. Thinking O(n) is always faster than O(n^2) for every input size; for small n, a Theta(n^2) algorithm with tiny constants can win, which is why real libraries sometimes switch to insertion sort for small arrays. And mixing up O with Theta when the question asks for a tight bound.

What exams ask: State the formal definitions of O, Omega and Theta, and draw the classic picture where f(n) is squeezed between c1 g(n) and c2 g(n) after n0. Prove that a given polynomial is Theta(n^k) by finding constants. Prove that n^2 is not O(n). Arrange a list of functions in increasing order of growth, often including tricky ones like n^(log n), 2^(log n) which equals n, and log(n!). Decide true or false for statements like 2^(n+1) = O(2^n).

Recap: Asymptotic notation describes how cost grows for large n by keeping the dominant term and ignoring constants. O is an upper bound, Omega a lower bound, Theta a tight bound, and little-o and little-omega are strict versions. You can prove bounds with explicit c and n0 or with the limit trick, and you should know the growth ladder by heart. With this language ready, the next lesson shows how to actually count the steps of real code.
key_points: f = O(g): there exist c > 0 and n0 with f(n) <= c g(n) for all n >= n0 (upper bound).
f = Omega(g): f(n) >= c g(n) for large n (lower bound); f = Theta(g) means both hold (tight bound).
Little-o and little-omega are strict versions: grows strictly slower or strictly faster.
Limit of f/g: 0 means o, a positive constant means Theta, infinity means omega.
Growth ladder: 1 < log n < sqrt n < n < n log n < n^2 < n^3 < 2^n < n! < n^n.
Log bases do not matter asymptotically, but exponential bases do (4^n is not O(2^n)).
Asymptotic notation and best/worst/average case are separate ideas.
lessons.tip: When proving a bound, replace every lower term by the biggest term to find c quickly; for disproving, assume c and n0 exist and hunt for an n that breaks the inequality.

lessons.title: Analysing Loops and Proving Correctness
lessons.content:
Imagine a tea stall near your campus. The owner wants to know how long it takes to serve a group. Pouring one cup takes a fixed time. Serving n friends takes n pours. If each friend also wants to clink cups with every other friend, that adds about n squared clinks. Without a stopwatch, just by looking at what is being done, he can predict how the time grows. That is exactly what we do with code: read the loops, count the work, and turn it into a growth rate using the notation from the last lesson.

The basic counting rules: A simple statement such as an assignment, a comparison or an arithmetic operation costs O(1). A sequence of blocks costs the sum of their costs, so by the sum rule it is dominated by the most expensive block. An if-else costs the test plus the more expensive branch, if we want a worst-case bound. A loop costs the number of iterations times the cost of one iteration, if every iteration costs the same; if not, we add up the cost of each iteration separately. A function call costs whatever the function costs.

A single loop: Consider: s = 0; for i = 1 to n: s = s + A[i]. The body runs exactly n times and costs a constant each time. So the total is c times n plus a constant for the setup, which is Theta(n). It does not matter that the body has two or three operations; that only changes the constant.

Loops with a step: What if the loop is for i = 1 to n step 2? It runs about n/2 times, still Theta(n). What about for i = 1 to n step 100? About n/100 times, still Theta(n). Changing the step by a constant only changes the constant factor. Students often get this wrong and write O(n/2), which is just O(n).

Independent nested loops: for i = 1 to n: for j = 1 to m: do O(1) work. The inner loop runs m times for each of the n values of i, giving n times m operations, Theta(nm). When m = n, it is Theta(n^2). A typical example is going through every cell of an n by m matrix, like a spreadsheet of marks with n students and m subjects.

Dependent nested loops: Now: for i = 1 to n: for j = 1 to i: do O(1) work. The inner loop runs 1 time, then 2 times, then 3, up to n. The total is 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2. That is about n^2/2, which is Theta(n^2). The same answer comes from for j = i + 1 to n, which runs n - 1, n - 2, ..., 0 times and sums to n(n - 1)/2. This pattern appears whenever we compare every pair of items once.

Doubling and halving loops: Consider: i = 1; while i < n: i = 2 * i. The values of i are 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on. After k rounds, i = 2^k, and the loop stops when 2^k >= n, that is, when k >= log2 n. So it runs about log2 n times, Theta(log n). Halving works the same: i = n; while i > 1: i = i / 2 also runs about log2 n times. This is why binary search is logarithmic: it halves the search range each step.

Combining them: for i = 1 to n: j = 1; while j < n: j = 2 * j. The outer loop runs n times and the inner one about log2 n times, independently, so the total is Theta(n log n). But be careful with dependency: for i = 1 to n: j = 1; while j < i: j = 2 * j gives log 1 + log 2 + ... + log n, which is log(n!), and we saw in lesson 2 that this is still Theta(n log n).

The harmonic surprise: Look at: for i = 1 to n: for j = 1 to n step i: O(1) work. When i = 1 the inner loop runs n times, when i = 2 about n/2 times, when i = 3 about n/3, and so on. The total is n times (1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ... + 1/n). The sum in brackets is the harmonic number H_n, which is about ln n. So the total is Theta(n log n), not n^2. This exact pattern shows up in the Sieve of Eratosthenes for finding primes.

The square root loop: i = 1; while i * i <= n: i = i + 1. The loop stops when i passes the square root of n, so it runs about square root of n times. Checking whether a number is prime by trying divisors up to its square root uses this loop. For n = 1,000,000 it is only 1000 checks.

Summation formulas you need: Arithmetic series: 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2, which is Theta(n^2). Sum of squares: 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + n^2 = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6, Theta(n^3). Geometric series: 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^k = 2^(k+1) - 1, so the sum is dominated by its last term. Harmonic series: 1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n is about ln n. With these four you can analyse almost every loop in the syllabus.

Insertion sort, the code: Insertion sort works like arranging playing cards in your hand. for i = 2 to n: key = A[i]; j = i - 1; while j >= 1 and A[j] > key: A[j + 1] = A[j]; j = j - 1; then A[j + 1] = key. Each new card is pushed left past all bigger cards until it finds its place.

Insertion sort, best case: If the array is already sorted, the while test fails immediately for every i, because A[i - 1] <= A[i]. So each of the n - 1 outer rounds does one comparison and no shifts. The total is n - 1 comparisons, Theta(n). This is why insertion sort is great for data that is almost sorted.

Insertion sort, worst case: If the array is sorted in reverse, every new key is smaller than all cards before it, so it shifts all the way to the front. For i = 2 it shifts 1 element, for i = 3 two elements, up to n - 1 for i = n. Total shifts: 1 + 2 + ... + (n - 1) = n(n - 1)/2, which is Theta(n^2). Try 4, 3, 2, 1: shifts are 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, and 4 times 3 divided by 2 = 6. It matches.

Insertion sort, average case: An inversion is a pair of positions i < j with A[i] > A[j]. Every shift of insertion sort fixes exactly one inversion. In a random order, each pair is inverted with probability one half, so the expected number of inversions is n(n - 1)/4. So the average case is also about n^2/4, which is Theta(n^2). Same growth as the worst case, half the constant.

Loop invariants, the correctness tool: A loop invariant is a statement that we prove in three parts. Initialization: it is true before the first iteration. Maintenance: if it is true before an iteration, it is still true before the next one. Termination: when the loop ends, the invariant plus the stopping condition gives us the result we wanted. It works just like mathematical induction from discrete maths.

The invariant for insertion sort: "At the start of each iteration with index i, the subarray A[1..i-1] contains the elements originally in A[1..i-1], but in sorted order." Initialization: when i = 2, A[1..1] has one element, which is trivially sorted. Maintenance: the inner loop shifts bigger elements one step right and drops key into the gap, so A[1..i] becomes sorted. Termination: the loop ends when i = n + 1, so A[1..n] is the whole array, sorted. Done.

Space complexity: Insertion sort uses only a few extra variables (key, i, j), no matter how big n is. Its extra space is O(1), and we call such algorithms in-place. Counting space works like counting time: count the extra memory cells as a function of n, ignoring the input itself. An algorithm that copies the array into a new one uses Theta(n) extra space.

Real-life example 1, attendance and copy-checking: A teacher calling roll for n students does Theta(n) work. Now suppose she wants to check whether any two students submitted the same assignment by comparing every pair. That is n(n - 1)/2 comparisons. For a class of 60 that is 1770 pairs, tiring but possible. For all 5000 students of a university it is about 12.5 million pairs, impossible by hand. A smarter way is to sort the assignments by some fingerprint first, so equal ones sit next to each other, which needs about n log n work.

Real-life example 2, playing taas: When friends deal cards for a game of 29 or call break, most people pick up cards one by one and slide each new card into its correct place among the cards already in hand. That is insertion sort. With 13 cards it feels instant. If you happened to receive the cards already in order, you would just place each at the end, the best case. If they came in exactly reverse order, every new card would travel to the far left, the worst case.

Common mistakes: Assuming two nested loops always mean n^2. If the inner loop doubles its counter, it is n log n; if it runs a fixed 10 times, it is just n. Forgetting that the inner loop count may depend on the outer variable. Writing the answer before simplifying sums, like leaving it as n(n + 1)/2 without saying Theta(n^2). And saying insertion sort is O(n) without saying "in the best case".

What exams ask: Find the time complexity of given code fragments, especially dependent loops, doubling loops and the harmonic loop. Analyse insertion sort in best, worst and average case with step counts. State and prove a loop invariant for insertion sort or for a simple sum or max loop. Explain what in-place means. Trace insertion sort on a small array and count the shifts.

Recap: To analyse iterative code, count iterations, multiply by the body cost, and add up blocks. Know the four sums: arithmetic, squares, geometric and harmonic. Doubling or halving gives log n, dependent loops usually give n^2/2, and step-by-i loops give n log n. Insertion sort is Theta(n) best, Theta(n^2) worst and average, and in-place. Loop invariants prove correctness in three steps. Next lesson: recursive code, where counting turns into solving recurrences.
key_points: Loop cost = number of iterations times cost per iteration; blocks in sequence add up.
Changing a loop step by a constant does not change Theta(n).
Doubling or halving a counter gives Theta(log n) iterations.
Dependent loops 1 + 2 + ... + n give Theta(n^2); the step-by-i loop gives the harmonic sum, Theta(n log n).
Insertion sort: Theta(n) best (sorted), Theta(n^2) worst (reverse) and average, O(1) extra space.
Each shift in insertion sort removes one inversion; random input has n(n - 1)/4 inversions on average.
A loop invariant is proved by initialization, maintenance and termination.
lessons.tip: Before writing any Big-O, write a tiny table: value of the outer variable on the left, how many times the inner loop runs on the right. Then add the right column. Most mistakes vanish.
lessons.task: Take 6 playing cards or 6 pieces of paper numbered 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. Sort them with insertion sort by hand and count every shift. Check that you get 15 = 6 times 5 divided by 2.

quiz.explain: i doubles each round, so about log2 n rounds.

for i = 1 to n: for j = 1 to n step i: O(1). Total work?
quiz.explain: n(1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n) is n times the harmonic number, about n ln n.

quiz.explain: Then the inner loop never shifts, giving n - 1 comparisons.
