quiz.explain: The three parts are initialization, maintenance and termination.

lessons.title: Recurrences I: Writing and Solving by Hand
lessons.content:
Imagine you ask your little brother how many stairs there are up to the roof of your building. He is lazy, so he says: "I will climb one stair, and then ask the stair below me to count the rest." Every helper does one stair of work and passes the rest of the job on. The total effort is one plus the effort of the smaller job. That little sentence, "the cost of a big job equals some small work plus the cost of smaller jobs", is exactly what a recurrence is. In this lesson we learn to write recurrences from recursive code and solve them with three hand methods: substitution, iteration (unrolling) and the recursion tree. The master theorem, a fast shortcut, comes in the next lesson.

What a recurrence is: A recurrence is an equation that describes a function in terms of its own value on smaller inputs. For running time we usually write T(n) for the time on an input of size n. Example: T(n) = T(n-1) + c for n > 1, and T(1) = c. The second part is called the base case, and it is important: without it the equation never stops, just like a recursive function without a base case runs forever.

Why we need them: In lesson 3 we counted loops. But recursive code has no visible loop. Binary search, merge sort and quick sort call themselves, so the cost hides inside the calls. The recurrence turns that hidden cost into maths. Once we solve it, we get a normal answer like Theta(n log n) that we can compare with other algorithms.

Reading code into a recurrence, rule one: Look at the function and ask three questions. How many recursive calls does it make? On what size is each call? How much work happens outside the calls (splitting, combining, looping)? Then write T(n) = (sum of the costs of the calls) + (outside work). Finally write the base case, usually T(1) = constant.

Example one, recursive sum: sum(A, n): if n == 0 return 0; return A[n] + sum(A, n-1). One call on size n-1, plus constant work. So T(n) = T(n-1) + c and T(0) = c.

Example two, binary search: search(lo, hi): if lo > hi return not found; mid = (lo+hi)/2; compare; then search only one half. One call on size n/2, plus constant work. So T(n) = T(n/2) + c.

Example three, merge sort: sort the left half, sort the right half, merge the two in linear time. Two calls on size n/2, plus about n work. So T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn.

Example four, a tricky one: fib(n): if n <= 1 return n; return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2). Two calls, but on sizes n-1 and n-2, plus constant work. So T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + c. This grows exponentially, which is why naive Fibonacci is so slow. We will fix it with dynamic programming later in the course.

Floors and small details: Real code splits n into floor(n/2) and ceil(n/2), not perfectly into n/2. For asymptotic answers we usually ignore floors and ceilings and assume n is a nice power of 2. It almost never changes the Theta answer, and textbooks like CLRS show why. Also the exact constant c does not matter for Theta, so many people write T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n directly.

Method one, iteration or unrolling: The simplest idea. Keep replacing T of a smaller size by its own formula until you see a pattern, then jump to the base case. Take T(n) = T(n-1) + 1 with T(1) = 1. T(n) = T(n-1) + 1 = T(n-2) + 2 = T(n-3) + 3. After k steps, T(n) = T(n-k) + k. Stop when n-k = 1, so k = n-1. Then T(n) = T(1) + n - 1 = n. Answer: Theta(n).

Unrolling binary search: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 = T(n/4) + 2 = T(n/8) + 3. After k steps, T(n) = T(n/2^k) + k. Stop when n/2^k = 1, so k = log2 n. Then T(n) = T(1) + log2 n, which is Theta(log n). This is the formal proof of why binary search is so fast.

Unrolling with growing work: T(n) = T(n-1) + n, T(1) = 1. T(n) = n + (n-1) + T(n-2) = n + (n-1) + (n-2) + T(n-3), and so on down to 1. The total is 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2, which is Theta(n^2). This recurrence describes selection sort written recursively, and also quick sort in its worst case.

Unrolling with doubling: T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1, T(0) = 0. T(n) = 2(2T(n-2) + 1) + 1 = 4T(n-2) + 2 + 1 = 8T(n-3) + 4 + 2 + 1. After n steps, T(n) = 2^n T(0) + (2^(n-1) + ... + 2 + 1) = 2^n - 1. This is the famous Tower of Hanoi count: to move n discs you need 2^n - 1 moves. With 64 discs that is more moves than anyone could ever finish.

Method two, the recursion tree: Unrolling becomes messy when there are two or more calls. A picture helps. Draw the root as the outside work of the top call. Its children are the outside work of each recursive call, and so on down to the leaves, which are base cases. Then add up each level, and add up all the levels.

Recursion tree for merge sort: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. Root does n work. Level 1 has 2 nodes of size n/2, each doing n/2, total n. Level 2 has 4 nodes of size n/4, total n. Level i has 2^i nodes each doing n/2^i, total n again. The tree goes down until size 1, which takes log2 n levels, plus the leaf level. So the total is about n times (log2 n + 1), which is Theta(n log n). Every level costs the same, so the answer is (work per level) times (number of levels).

Recursion tree when the root dominates: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n^2. Root costs n^2. Level 1: two nodes each (n/2)^2 = n^2/4, total n^2/2. Level 2: four nodes each n^2/16, total n^2/4. The level costs shrink by half each time: n^2 + n^2/2 + n^2/4 + ... is a decreasing geometric series, which is at most 2n^2. So T(n) = Theta(n^2). The top level wins.

Recursion tree when the leaves dominate: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n. Root costs n. Level 1: four nodes of n/2, total 2n. Level 2: sixteen nodes of n/4, total 4n. Costs double each level. The last level has 4^(log2 n) = n^2 leaves, so the leaves cost Theta(n^2) and the whole sum is Theta(n^2). Here the bottom wins. Notice the pattern: same level cost gives an extra log factor, shrinking costs means the root wins, growing costs means the leaves win. Remember this, because the master theorem in the next lesson is exactly this idea written as a rule.

Uneven splits: T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n. The tree is lopsided: the left branch reaches size 1 after log3 n levels, the right branch after log base 3/2 of n levels. Every full level still costs at most n. The number of levels is at most log base 3/2 of n, which is Theta(log n). So T(n) = O(n log n), and a similar lower count gives Omega(n log n). This explains why quick sort is still Theta(n log n) even if every pivot splits 1:2 instead of in half.

Method three, substitution: This is the rigorous method. Step one: guess the form of the answer, often from a recursion tree. Step two: prove it by mathematical induction, using the recurrence. Example: show T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n is O(n log n). Guess T(n) <= c n log2 n for some constant c. Assume it holds for n/2, so T(n/2) <= c (n/2) log2(n/2). Then T(n) <= 2 c (n/2) (log2 n - 1) + n = c n log2 n - c n + n. This is at most c n log2 n whenever c >= 1. The induction step works, and we pick base cases (like n = 2) to make the start true.

A trap in substitution: Suppose someone guesses T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n is O(n) and writes T(n) <= 2 c (n/2) + n = cn + n = O(n). Wrong! The induction must prove the exact same form, T(n) <= cn, but we got cn + n, which is bigger than cn. You cannot let the constant grow at every step. Examiners love this trap.

Subtracting a lower-order term: Sometimes the right guess fails by a tiny bit. For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1, guessing T(n) <= cn gives cn + 1, which is not <= cn. The trick is to make the guess stronger: T(n) <= cn - d. Then T(n) <= 2(c n/2 - d) + 1 = cn - 2d + 1, which is <= cn - d when d >= 1. A stronger statement can be easier to prove by induction, which surprises many students.

Changing variables: Some recurrences look strange, like T(n) = 2T(sqrt n) + log n. Put m = log2 n, so n = 2^m and sqrt n = 2^(m/2). Let S(m) = T(2^m). Then S(m) = 2S(m/2) + m, which is merge sort's recurrence, so S(m) = Theta(m log m). Changing back, T(n) = Theta(log n times log log n). A clever renaming turns an unfamiliar problem into a familiar one.

Real life example one, Dhaka phone tree: A school in Dhaka needs to tell 1,024 parents that school is closed because of rain. The headteacher calls 2 class teachers, each calls 2 more, and so on. If each call takes 1 minute and calls happen in parallel, the time is T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 minutes in the waiting sense, which unrolls to log2 1024 = 10 rounds. Ten minutes for everybody, instead of 1,024 minutes if one person called all parents. Recurrences explain why a tree of helpers is so powerful.

Real life example two, sorting exam scripts: A teacher at a Rajshahi college has 800 answer scripts to sort by roll number. She splits the pile in two, gives each half to an assistant, and asks them to do the same. At the end, every pair of sorted piles is merged by walking through both. Merging two piles of total size m takes about m steps. That is merge sort in real life, and the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n tells her the total effort is about 800 times log2 800, which is roughly 800 times 10 = 8,000 basic steps, much less than the 320,000 comparisons a careless pairwise method would need.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the base case. Writing T(n) = T(n/2) + T(n/2) + n but then counting only one call. Mixing up "number of calls" (the a in front) with "size of each call" (the n/b inside). Thinking the recurrence T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) is polynomial; it is exponential. In substitution proofs, letting the constant grow. In recursion trees, forgetting the leaf level when the leaves dominate.

What exams ask: Write the recurrence for a given piece of recursive code. Solve T(n) = T(n-1) + n, T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1, T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 by iteration. Draw the recursion tree for T(n) = 3T(n/4) + n^2 or T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n and give a tight bound. Prove a bound by substitution. These are very common in BUET, DU and KUET term finals.

Recap: A recurrence writes the cost of a recursive algorithm in terms of smaller costs. Read code by counting calls, sub-problem sizes and outside work. Unrolling works best with one call. Recursion trees show the work level by level and tell you whether the root, the leaves, or every level equally dominates. Substitution turns a guess into a proof by induction. Next lesson, the master theorem gives instant answers for the most common shape, T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n).
key_points: A recurrence describes a cost in terms of the same cost on smaller inputs, plus a base case.
From code: count the recursive calls, the size of each call, and the work outside the calls.
Unrolling (iteration) works best with a single recursive call: T(n)=T(n-1)+1 is n, T(n)=T(n/2)+1 is log n.
A recursion tree adds work level by level: equal levels give an extra log factor, shrinking levels mean the root dominates, growing levels mean the leaves dominate.
Substitution = guess the form, then prove it by induction with the exact same constant.
T(n)=2T(n-1)+1 gives 2^n - 1 (Tower of Hanoi); T(n)=T(n-1)+n gives Theta(n^2).
lessons.tip: When a recurrence looks scary, draw just the first three levels of its recursion tree and write the total under each level. The pattern usually jumps out.
lessons.task: Take Tower of Hanoi with 3 discs (use three coins of different sizes). Count the moves and check that you get 2^3 - 1 = 7. Then write the recurrence for n discs.

quiz.q: If a recursive function makes two calls on halves and does linear extra work, which recurrence fits?
quiz.explain: Two calls on size n/2 give 2T(n/2), and the linear merge-style work adds n.

quiz.q: Unrolling T(n) = T(n-1) + 1 with T(1) = 1 gives what?
quiz.explain: Each step adds 1 and there are about n steps, so T(n) = n.

quiz.q: In the recursion tree of T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, how much work is done on each level?
quiz.explain: Level i has 2^i nodes, each doing n/2^i work, so every level costs n.

quiz.q: What is the solution of T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1 with T(0) = 0?
quiz.explain: Unrolling gives 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^(n-1) = 2^n - 1, like the Tower of Hanoi.

quiz.q: In the substitution method, what do you do after guessing T(n) <= c n log n?
options: Run the program for big n
Prove the guess by induction, plugging it into the recurrence
Assume the answer is always Theta(n)
quiz.explain: Substitution means guess the form, then prove it by induction using the recurrence.

lessons.title: Recurrences II: The Master Theorem
lessons.content:
Imagine your school has a big exam paper checking job. The head teacher splits the pile of papers into equal parts and gives one part to each of a few teachers. Each teacher does the same: splits their pile and passes it on, until somebody holds just one paper and checks it. At every step there is also some extra work: handing out piles and collecting marks. How long does the whole job take? In lesson 4 we answered questions like this by drawing recursion trees by hand. That works, but it is slow. The master theorem is the shortcut: for a very common family of recurrences, you just compare two things and read off the answer in a few seconds.

The shape it handles: The master theorem works for recurrences of the form T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n), where a >= 1 and b > 1 are constants and f(n) is a positive function. Read it like a story. The problem of size n is split into a subproblems. Each subproblem has size n/b. The extra work done at this level, for splitting and combining, is f(n). Merge sort is a = 2, b = 2, f(n) = n. Binary search is a = 1, b = 2, f(n) = 1. Karatsuba multiplication is a = 3, b = 2, f(n) = n.

The magic number: Before using any case, compute the critical exponent log_b(a), the logarithm of a in base b. Then n^(log_b a) tells you how many leaves the recursion tree has. Why? The tree has depth log_b(n), and at each level the number of nodes multiplies by a, so the number of leaves is a^(log_b n), which equals n^(log_b a). For merge sort, log_2(2) = 1, so there are n leaves. For binary search, log_2(1) = 0, so n^0 = 1 leaf. For Karatsuba, log_2(3) is about 1.585, so about n^1.585 leaves.

The tug of war: Think of the total work as a tug of war between two teams. Team leaves pulls with n^(log_b a), the total work done at the bottom. Team root pulls with f(n), the work done at the top. Whichever team is polynomially stronger wins and decides the answer. If they are equal, the work is the same on every level, and since there are about log n levels, you get an extra log n factor. That is the whole idea; the three cases below are just this tug of war written carefully.

Case 1, leaves win: If f(n) = O(n^(log_b a - e)) for some constant e > 0, meaning f grows polynomially slower than n^(log_b a), then T(n) = Theta(n^(log_b a)). The work keeps growing as you go down the tree, and the bottom level dominates. Example: T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n^2. Here log_2(8) = 3, so leaves give n^3. f(n) = n^2 is n^(3-1), polynomially smaller with e = 1. Answer: Theta(n^3). This is exactly the simple recursive matrix multiplication with eight half-size products.

Case 2, a tie: If f(n) = Theta(n^(log_b a)), then T(n) = Theta(n^(log_b a) log n). Every level of the tree does about the same work, and there are about log n levels. Example: merge sort, T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. log_2(2) = 1, f(n) = n = n^1. Tie, so Theta(n log n). Another example: binary search, T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. log_2(1) = 0, n^0 = 1, f(n) = 1. Tie again, so Theta(log n). Many students are surprised that binary search is a case 2 example, but it fits perfectly.

Case 3, root wins: If f(n) = Omega(n^(log_b a + e)) for some constant e > 0, and also the regularity condition holds, meaning a f(n/b) <= c f(n) for some constant c < 1 and all large n, then T(n) = Theta(f(n)). The work shrinks as you go down, so the top level dominates. Example: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n^2. log_2(2) = 1, f(n) = n^2 is n^(1+1), polynomially bigger. Check regularity: 2 (n/2)^2 = n^2/2, which is (1/2) n^2, and 1/2 < 1. So T(n) = Theta(n^2).

Why the regularity condition: The regularity condition says that the total work at the next level down is a fixed fraction smaller than this level. Then the level costs form a decreasing geometric series, and the sum of a decreasing geometric series is a constant times its first term, which is f(n). For normal polynomial functions like n^2 or n^3 it is always true, so in exams you just show the one-line check. It matters for strange functions that wobble up and down.

A step by step recipe: Step 1, write a, b and f(n). Step 2, compute log_b(a) and write n^(log_b a). Step 3, compare f(n) with it: smaller by a polynomial factor, equal, or bigger by a polynomial factor. Step 4, for case 3, check regularity. Step 5, write the answer with Theta. Do this in the same order every time and you will rarely make mistakes.

Worked example A: T(n) = 9T(n/3) + n. a = 9, b = 3, log_3(9) = 2, so compare n with n^2. f(n) = n = n^(2-1), smaller with e = 1. Case 1. Answer Theta(n^2).

Worked example B: T(n) = T(2n/3) + 1. a = 1, b = 3/2. log_(3/2)(1) = 0, so n^0 = 1. f(n) = 1. Tie, case 2. Answer Theta(log n). Notice b does not need to be a whole number, it only needs to be bigger than 1.

Worked example C: T(n) = 3T(n/4) + n log n. a = 3, b = 4, log_4(3) is about 0.793. f(n) = n log n is bigger than n^0.793 by more than a polynomial factor; take e = 0.2 and n log n is still Omega(n^0.993). Regularity: 3 (n/4) log(n/4) <= (3/4) n log n, and 3/4 < 1. Case 3, answer Theta(n log n).

Worked example D: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n^2. a = 4, b = 2, log_2(4) = 2. f(n) = n^2. Tie. Answer Theta(n^2 log n). And T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n^3 gives case 3: Theta(n^3). While T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n gives case 1: Theta(n^2). Same a and b, three different answers, all decided by f(n).

When the master theorem fails, gap one: The comparison must be polynomial. Look at T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n. n^(log_2 2) = n, and f(n) = n log n is bigger than n, but only by a log factor, not by n^e for any e > 0. So it falls in the gap between case 2 and case 3, and the basic master theorem does not apply. Using a recursion tree, every level costs about n log(n/2^i), and the sum is Theta(n log^2 n). An extended version of case 2 covers this: if f(n) = Theta(n^(log_b a) log^k n) with k >= 0, then T(n) = Theta(n^(log_b a) log^(k+1) n).

When it fails, gap two: The shape must match. T(n) = T(n-1) + n is not a T(n/b) form; the problem shrinks by subtraction, not division. Use unrolling: the answer is Theta(n^2). T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1 is also outside; it is Tower of Hanoi and equals 2^n - 1. T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n has two different sizes, so again no master theorem; a recursion tree shows each full level costs n, the depth is about log_(3/2) n, so the answer is Theta(n log n). For these uneven splits, a more general tool called the Akra-Bazzi method exists, but you only need to know its name at this level.

When it fails, gap three: a must be a constant at least 1, and b must be a constant bigger than 1. T(n) = 2^n T(n/2) + n is not allowed because a depends on n. T(n) = 0.5 T(n/2) + n is not allowed because a < 1. In exams, a question that says 'can the master theorem be applied? Explain' is usually one of these traps.

A common recurrences table: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 gives Theta(log n), binary search. T(n) = T(n/2) + n gives Theta(n), like quickselect when it is lucky. T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1 gives Theta(n), like a recursive tree traversal or finding the max by halves. T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n gives Theta(n log n), merge sort. T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n gives Theta(n^1.585), Karatsuba. T(n) = 7T(n/2) + n^2 gives Theta(n^2.81), Strassen. T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n^2 gives Theta(n^3), plain recursive matrix multiply. T(n) = T(n-1) + 1 gives Theta(n). T(n) = T(n-1) + n gives Theta(n^2). T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1 gives Theta(2^n). Learn this table well; it saves time in every later lesson.

Real life example 1, a mobile company's billing: Suppose a telecom company in Dhaka has to total the bills of n customers. One design: a manager splits the list into 2 halves, gives each to a team, and adds the two totals at the end, which is constant work. T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1, case 1 with log_2 2 = 1 beating f(n) = 1, so Theta(n). Fine, everyone gets added once. Now a worse design: at each level the manager also re-reads all records to double check them, which is n work. T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, which is Theta(n log n). The master theorem tells the company, in seconds, how much the double checking costs.

Real life example 2, an image filter on your phone: Many photo apps shrink a picture into quarters, process each quarter, and then blend the edges. If they split into 4 quarters of half width and half height, the number of pixels in each part is n/4, where n is the total number of pixels. With blending work proportional to the pixels, T(n) = 4T(n/4) + n. log_4(4) = 1, tie, so Theta(n log n). If an engineer found a trick to need only 3 of the 4 quarters, T(n) = 3T(n/4) + n would be case 3, just Theta(n). Small changes in a or f(n) can change the speed class.

Common mistakes: First, comparing f(n) with n instead of with n^(log_b a). Always compute the critical exponent first. Second, forgetting the word polynomially: n log n versus n is not case 3. Third, forgetting the regularity check in case 3. Fourth, using the theorem on T(n-1) style recurrences. Fifth, mixing up a and b: in 3T(n/4), a = 3 and b = 4, so the exponent is log_4 3, not log_3 4.

What exams ask: Typical questions are 'solve these five recurrences using the master theorem, mention the case', 'state the master theorem', 'give an example where it cannot be applied and solve it another way', and 'the running time of algorithm X is T(n) = 7T(n/2) + n^2, what is its complexity?'. If you can do the five-step recipe quickly and know the three gaps, you are ready.

Recap: The master theorem solves T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n) by a tug of war between the leaves, n^(log_b a), and the root work, f(n). Leaves stronger gives Theta(n^(log_b a)), equal gives an extra log n, root stronger gives Theta(f(n)) with regularity. It does not cover subtraction recurrences, uneven splits, or comparisons that differ only by log factors. Next lesson we use these tools on real divide and conquer algorithms.
key_points: The master theorem solves T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n) with a >= 1, b > 1.
First compute n^(log_b a), the number of leaves of the recursion tree.
Case 1: f(n) polynomially smaller, answer Theta(n^(log_b a)).
Case 2: f(n) equal, answer Theta(n^(log_b a) log n).
Case 3: f(n) polynomially bigger plus regularity, answer Theta(f(n)).
It fails for subtraction recurrences, uneven splits, non-constant a, and log-factor gaps like 2T(n/2) + n log n.
Memorise the common table: binary search log n, merge sort n log n, Karatsuba n^1.585, Strassen n^2.81.
lessons.tip: Always write the five steps in the same order: a, b, f(n); n^(log_b a); compare; regularity if case 3; answer. Speed comes from routine.
lessons.task: Solve these on paper with the master theorem and name the case: T(n)=4T(n/2)+n, T(n)=4T(n/2)+n^2, T(n)=4T(n/2)+n^3, T(n)=T(n/2)+n. Then check one of them by drawing three levels of the recursion tree.

quiz.q: For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, which case of the master theorem applies and what is T(n)?
quiz.explain: n^(log_2 2) = n equals f(n), a tie, so Theta(n log n).

quiz.q: What is n^(log_b a) for T(n) = 9T(n/3) + n?
quiz.explain: log_3 9 = 2, so the leaves give n^2; f(n) = n is smaller, case 1, Theta(n^2).

quiz.q: Why can the basic master theorem not solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n?
options: Because n log n is bigger than n only by a log factor, not polynomially
Because b is not an integer
Because it is a subtraction recurrence
quiz.explain: It falls in the gap between case 2 and case 3; the answer is Theta(n log^2 n).

quiz.q: Which recurrence is outside the master theorem's form?
quiz.explain: T(n-1) shrinks by subtraction, not division; unrolling gives Theta(n^2).

quiz.q: What extra condition does case 3 require?
options: Regularity: a f(n/b) <= c f(n) for some c < 1
quiz.explain: Regularity makes level costs a decreasing geometric series so the root dominates.

lessons.title: Divide and Conquer: Merge Sort, Max Subarray, Inversions
lessons.content:
Imagine your class has to clean the whole school before Victory Day. If one student tries to do it alone, it takes forever. The class captain has a better plan: split the school into floors, give each floor to a group, each group splits its floor into rooms, and each pair of students cleans one room. At the end, the groups report back and the captain puts the full report together. That plan has three steps: divide the big job, conquer the small jobs, and combine the results. This is the divide and conquer paradigm, one of the most powerful ideas in algorithm design.

The paradigm: A divide and conquer algorithm has three parts. Divide: break the problem into smaller subproblems of the same type. Conquer: solve each subproblem recursively; when a subproblem is tiny, solve it directly (the base case). Combine: join the sub-answers into the answer for the original problem. The running time almost always looks like T(n) = a T(n/b) + D(n) + C(n), where D(n) is the divide cost and C(n) is the combine cost. That is exactly the shape the master theorem from lesson 5 eats for breakfast.

Where the cleverness lives: In some algorithms the divide step is trivial and the combine step is smart (merge sort). In others the divide step is smart and the combine step is trivial (quick sort, next lesson). Some have almost no combine at all (binary search). When you design a new D&C algorithm, ask: what must the combine step do, and can it be done fast? Usually the whole difficulty is in that one step.

Merge sort, the algorithm: To sort A[1..n]: if n is 1, it is already sorted. Otherwise split at the middle, recursively sort the left half and the right half, then merge the two sorted halves. Merging uses two pointers, i on the left half and j on the right. Compare L[i] and R[j], copy the smaller to the output, move that pointer forward. When one half runs out, copy the rest of the other. Example: merging [2, 5, 9] and [3, 4, 10] gives 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, with at most 5 comparisons for 6 items.

Merge sort, the analysis: Merging two lists with a total of n items takes at most n - 1 comparisons, so the combine cost is Theta(n). The divide cost is just computing the middle, Theta(1). So T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n), which is Theta(n log n) by master theorem case 2. Using the recursion tree: there are log2(n) levels, and each level merges a total of n items, so the total is about n log2 n. For n = 1,024, that is about 10,240 basic steps, compared with about 500,000 for a quadratic sort.

Merge sort, the properties: It is Theta(n log n) in the best, worst and average case; it does not care whether the input is already sorted. It is stable if the merge takes from the left half when values are equal, so equal keys keep their order. Its weakness is memory: the usual array version needs Theta(n) extra space for merging, so it is not in-place. On linked lists it can merge without extra arrays, which is why it is the favourite for sorting linked lists, and it is also the basis of external sorting of huge files that do not fit in RAM.

Merge in pseudo-code: merge(L, R): i = 0, j = 0, out = empty. While i < len(L) and j < len(R): if L[i] <= R[j], append L[i] and i = i + 1, else append R[j] and j = j + 1. After the loop, append whatever is left of L, then whatever is left of R. Return out. Notice the <= in the comparison. If you write < instead, equal items get taken from the right first, and merge sort stops being stable. It is a one-character difference that examiners like to ask about.

Divide and conquer and parallel computers: Because the subproblems in D&C are independent, they can be solved at the same time on different processor cores. Your phone probably has 8 cores. Sorting the left half and the right half of an array on two cores at once roughly halves the time of the top level. Big data systems take this further, splitting a job across hundreds of machines and combining the partial results, which is the same three-step idea at a much larger scale. So learning D&C also prepares you for parallel and distributed computing courses later.

Correctness of merge sort: Proof is by strong induction on n. Base: an array of size 1 is sorted. Step: assume the algorithm sorts every array smaller than n. Both halves are smaller, so they come back sorted. The merge loop keeps the invariant 'the output so far contains the smallest k items in sorted order', because each time it takes the smallest remaining item, which must be at the front of one of the two halves. When the loop ends, all n items are output in order.

Binary search as divide and conquer: Searching for x in a sorted array: compare x with the middle element. If equal, done. If x is smaller, search the left half, else the right half. Divide is the comparison, conquer is one recursive call, and combine is nothing: the answer of the half is the answer. T(n) = T(n/2) + Theta(1) = Theta(log n). For 1,000,000 items, that is at most 20 comparisons. It shows that a D&C algorithm does not need to solve every piece; sometimes you throw half the problem away.

Maximum subarray, the problem: Given an array of numbers that can be negative, find the contiguous part with the largest sum. Example: profit and loss of a small shop over 9 days: [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]. The best run is days 4 to 7, [4, -1, 2, 1], with sum 6. The brute force way checks every pair (i, j), which is Theta(n^2) pairs even with running sums.

Maximum subarray, the D&C idea: Split the array at the middle. The best subarray is either entirely in the left half, entirely in the right half, or it crosses the middle. The first two are found recursively. The crossing one is found directly: start at the middle and walk left, keeping the best sum of A[i..mid]; walk right keeping the best sum of A[mid+1..j]; add the two bests. That walk is Theta(n). Answer: the largest of the three. So T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n) = Theta(n log n), much better than n^2.

A note on Kadane: There is also a Theta(n) algorithm for maximum subarray, called Kadane's algorithm: keep the best sum ending at the current position, which is max(A[i], previous + A[i]), and keep the overall best. It is really a tiny dynamic programming idea. Exams often ask for the D&C version to test the crossing-sum idea, and then ask whether you can do better; the answer is yes, linear time with Kadane.

Counting inversions, the problem: An inversion in an array is a pair of positions i < j with A[i] > A[j]. It measures how unsorted the array is. A sorted array has 0 inversions, a reverse-sorted array of n items has n(n-1)/2. Example: [2, 4, 1, 3, 5] has inversions (2,1), (4,1), (4,3), so 3. Music and movie apps use this idea to compare two people's rankings: fewer inversions means more similar taste.

Counting inversions, the D&C trick: Split in half. Inversions are of three kinds: both in the left, both in the right, or split (one in each half). Count the first two recursively. For split inversions, piggyback on merge sort. While merging the sorted halves, whenever you take an element R[j] from the right half while i items remain in the left half, then R[j] is smaller than all those remaining left items, so it forms exactly that many split inversions. Add them up. The merge stays Theta(n), so the whole thing is Theta(n log n).

Worked inversion example: Left sorted [2, 4], right sorted [1, 3, 5]. Merge: compare 2 and 1, take 1 from the right while 2 items (2 and 4) remain on the left, add 2. Compare 2 and 3, take 2. Compare 4 and 3, take 3 from the right while 1 item (4) remains, add 1. Take 4, then 5. Split inversions = 3. Together with 0 inside each half, the total is 3, matching our hand count.

Real life example 1, a nationwide result sheet: Suppose the education board must sort the scores of 2 million SSC candidates. Each district office sorts its own list, sends it to the division, the division merges the district lists, and the board merges the 8 division lists. This is merge sort spread across offices. Each merge is linear in the number of names, and the total effort grows like n log n, so the work stays manageable even with millions of students.

Real life example 2, comparing tastes on a music app: You and your friend each rank 6 Bangla bands from favourite to least favourite. Write your friend's ranking using your positions, for example [2, 1, 4, 3, 6, 5]. Inversions are (2,1), (4,3), (6,5), so 3 out of a possible 15. That is a low number, so your tastes are close. A recommendation engine does this for millions of users, and the n log n inversion count makes it fast.

Choosing the base case: In practice, recursing down to size 1 wastes time on function calls. Real libraries switch to insertion sort when a piece is small, around 16 to 32 items, because insertion sort is very fast on tiny arrays. This does not change the Theta(n log n) bound, it only improves the constant. Python's built-in sort, Timsort, is a merge sort hybrid that uses this idea along with detecting already sorted runs.

Common mistakes: First, writing T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1 for merge sort, forgetting that merging costs Theta(n). Second, forgetting the crossing case in maximum subarray, or computing it as max of left plus max of right, which is wrong because the crossing piece must touch the middle. Third, in inversions, adding only 1 instead of the number of items remaining in the left half. Fourth, saying merge sort is in-place; the standard array version is not.

What exams ask: 'Write the three steps of divide and conquer.' 'Write the recurrence of merge sort and solve it.' 'Show the merge steps on this array.' 'Design an O(n log n) algorithm for maximum subarray and explain the crossing case.' 'Count inversions in [3, 1, 2, 5, 4] using merge sort.' Practise tracing by hand; examiners love step-by-step tables.

Recap: Divide and conquer means divide, conquer recursively, combine. Merge sort does trivial division and a linear merge, giving Theta(n log n) in all cases, stable but not in-place. Binary search throws half away, giving Theta(log n). Maximum subarray adds a linear crossing check, giving Theta(n log n). Counting inversions piggybacks on merging, also Theta(n log n). Next lesson we meet quick sort, where the cleverness moves from combine to divide.
key_points: Divide and conquer = divide into subproblems, conquer recursively, combine the answers.
Running time usually has the form T(n) = a T(n/b) + divide cost + combine cost.
Merge sort: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n) = Theta(n log n) in every case; stable, not in-place.
Binary search is D&C with one subproblem and no combine: Theta(log n).
Maximum subarray: best is left, right, or crossing the middle; crossing takes Theta(n); total Theta(n log n).
Counting inversions piggybacks on merge: add the number of items left in the left half when taking from the right.
Real libraries switch to insertion sort for tiny pieces to cut the constant.
lessons.tip: For every D&C algorithm, write one line each for divide, conquer and combine before writing code. If you cannot say what combine does, the design is not ready.
lessons.task: On paper, merge sort [5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3, 7, 4] and draw the full split-and-merge tree. While merging, count split inversions and check your total against a direct count of all pairs.

quiz.q: What are the three steps of divide and conquer?
quiz.explain: Break into subproblems, solve them recursively, join the answers.

quiz.q: Which recurrence describes merge sort?
quiz.explain: Two half-size sorts plus a linear merge, giving Theta(n log n).

quiz.q: In the D&C maximum subarray algorithm, how long does finding the best crossing subarray take?
quiz.explain: Walk left and right from the middle once each, which is linear.

quiz.q: How many inversions does [3, 1, 2] have?
quiz.explain: Pairs (3,1) and (3,2) are out of order; (1,2) is fine.

quiz.q: Which statement about standard array merge sort is true?
options: It is stable and needs Theta(n) extra space
It is fastest on reverse-sorted input only
quiz.explain: Merging into a temporary array needs linear extra space; taking left on ties keeps it stable.

lessons.title: Quick Sort: Partitions, Cases and Randomization
lessons.content:
Imagine a teacher lining up a class by height for the school assembly. She picks one student, say Rafi, and says: everyone shorter than Rafi stand on his left, everyone taller on his right. Now Rafi is standing exactly where he belongs in the final line, and she has two smaller groups to sort. She repeats the trick with each group. No merging is needed at the end, because the groups are already in the right order relative to each other. That is quick sort: the clever work happens while dividing, not while combining.

The algorithm: quicksort(A, lo, hi): if lo < hi: p = partition(A, lo, hi); quicksort(A, lo, p - 1); quicksort(A, p + 1, hi). The partition step chooses a pivot element and rearranges the subarray so that everything smaller or equal goes before the pivot and everything bigger goes after it, then returns the pivot's final index. Divide is partition (Theta(n)), conquer is two recursive calls, combine is nothing at all. Quick sort was invented by Tony Hoare around 1959 to 1961 and is still one of the most used sorts in the world.

Lomuto partition: This is the easy-to-learn version used in CLRS. Pick the last element as the pivot x. Keep an index i that marks the end of the 'small' zone, starting at lo - 1. Scan j from lo to hi - 1: if A[j] <= x, increase i and swap A[i] with A[j]. At the end, swap A[i+1] with A[hi] to put the pivot in place, and return i + 1. Invariant: A[lo..i] are all <= x, A[i+1..j-1] are all > x.

Lomuto worked example: A = [7, 2, 1, 8, 6, 3, 5, 4], pivot 4. i starts at -1 (0-based). j = 0: 7 > 4, skip. j = 1: 2 <= 4, i = 0, swap A[0] and A[1]: [2, 7, 1, 8, 6, 3, 5, 4]. j = 2: 1 <= 4, i = 1, swap: [2, 1, 7, 8, 6, 3, 5, 4]. j = 3, 4: 8 and 6 skip. j = 5: 3 <= 4, i = 2, swap A[2] and A[5]: [2, 1, 3, 8, 6, 7, 5, 4]. j = 6: 5 skip. Finally swap A[3] and the pivot: [2, 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 5, 8]. Return 3. The 4 is now in its final place.

Hoare partition: Hoare's original version uses two pointers moving towards each other. Pick the first element as the pivot. Pointer i moves right until it finds an element >= pivot; pointer j moves left until it finds an element <= pivot. If i < j, swap them and continue; otherwise return j. Hoare's version does about three times fewer swaps than Lomuto on average and handles many equal keys better. One catch: it returns a split point j, not the pivot's final position, so the recursive calls are on [lo..j] and [j+1..hi]. Mixing up this detail with Lomuto's recursion is a classic bug that causes infinite recursion.

Best case: If every partition splits the array exactly in half, T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n), which is Theta(n log n), the same as merge sort. In fact quick sort does not even need perfect halves. Even a split of 9 to 1 every time gives T(n) = T(9n/10) + T(n/10) + n. The recursion tree has depth log_(10/9) n, and each level costs at most n, so it is still Theta(n log n). Any split by a constant proportion is good enough.

Worst case: If the pivot is always the smallest or largest element, one side gets n - 1 items and the other gets 0. Then T(n) = T(n-1) + Theta(n), which unrolls to Theta(n^2). With 'last element as pivot', this happens on an already sorted array, which is ironic: the easiest input for a human is the worst input for this quick sort. It also happens when all elements are equal under Lomuto, because every element goes to the 'small' side.

Counting the worst case exactly: When every split is n - 1 and 0, the partition costs are n - 1, then n - 2, then n - 3, and so on down to 1 comparison. The sum is (n - 1) + (n - 2) + ... + 1 = n(n - 1)/2. For n = 1,000 that is 499,500 comparisons, while a balanced quick sort would need roughly 10,000. The same array, the same code, and a fifty times difference, only because of the pivot choice. This is why pivot selection is not a small detail but the heart of quick sort.

Why randomness helps, in plain words: Think of the pivot as a lottery ticket. A good pivot lands somewhere in the middle half of the values, between the 25th and 75th percentile. A random pivot is good with probability one half. Every good pivot shrinks the bigger side to at most three quarters of the size. So on average, every two levels you get at least one good shrink, and after about 2 log_(4/3) n levels the pieces are tiny. That is the intuition behind the expected O(n log n) bound without heavy probability.

Average case: If all input orders are equally likely, quick sort's expected running time is Theta(n log n). A neat way to see it: two elements are compared only if one of them is chosen as a pivot before any element with a value between them. The probability that the i-th and j-th smallest elements are compared is 2/(j - i + 1). Adding this up over all pairs gives about 2n ln n, which is about 1.39 n log2 n comparisons. That is only around 39 percent more comparisons than the best possible, and quick sort's simple inner loop makes up for it.

Randomized quick sort: We cannot control the input; an attacker or simply a sorted file can trigger the worst case. The fix is to pick the pivot at random: swap a random element of A[lo..hi] into the pivot position before partitioning. Now the expected running time is Theta(n log n) for every input, because the average is over our own coin flips, not over the inputs. The worst case is still Theta(n^2), but its probability is tiny. This is a Las Vegas algorithm: always the right answer, random running time. We meet this term again in lesson 26.

Other pivot tricks: Median of three picks the median of the first, middle and last elements, which fixes the sorted-input problem cheaply. For many equal keys, three-way partitioning (the Dutch national flag idea) splits into less than, equal to, and greater than the pivot, so a pile of equal items is finished in one pass. Introsort, used in C++ std::sort, starts with quick sort and switches to heap sort if the recursion gets too deep, which guarantees O(n log n) worst case.

In-place and stack space: Quick sort sorts inside the array, with only O(1) extra memory for partitioning. But recursion uses stack space: O(log n) in good cases and O(n) in the worst case. A standard trick is to recurse first on the smaller side and loop on the larger side; then the stack depth is always O(log n), even in a bad case.

Stability: Quick sort is not stable. Partition swaps elements across long distances, so two equal keys can change their relative order. Example: sorting students by marks, Anika (80) before Bithi (80) in the input might come out as Bithi before Anika. If you need stability, use merge sort, or add the original index as a tie breaker.

Quick sort versus merge sort: Both are Theta(n log n) on average. Merge sort guarantees it in the worst case, is stable, but needs Theta(n) extra memory. Quick sort is usually faster in practice on arrays because it works in place and its inner loop touches memory sequentially, which is cache friendly. But its worst case is Theta(n^2). That is why C++ uses introsort for std::sort, while Java uses a dual-pivot quick sort for primitive arrays and a merge sort based Timsort for objects, where stability matters.

A tiny correctness argument: After partition, the pivot is in its final sorted position, everything left of it is <= pivot and everything right is >= pivot. By induction, the recursive calls sort both sides. Since nothing ever needs to cross the pivot again, the whole array is sorted. This is why no combine step is required.

Real life example 1, a vegetable wholesaler at Karwan Bazar: A wholesaler has to sort a pile of sacks by weight. He picks one sack as a reference, puts lighter ones on the left and heavier on the right. The reference sack is now at its correct place. His helpers do the same with each side. If he always chooses the first sack from a line that was already sorted by a supplier, he gets the worst case and every split is lopsided. If he picks a random sack, the splits are usually reasonable and the job is fast. That is randomized quick sort in a bazaar.

Real life example 2, a food delivery app: Pathao or Foodpanda might sort thousands of restaurants by distance every second as users scroll. Engineers want speed and low memory on servers, so they use library sorts like introsort or pdqsort that start from quick sort ideas. When the app needs restaurants sorted by rating but keeping the distance order for equal ratings, they need a stable sort, so they choose a merge sort style algorithm instead. Knowing which sort is stable is a real engineering decision.

Common mistakes: First, saying quick sort's worst case is n log n; it is n^2. Second, believing randomization changes the worst case; it changes the expected time for every input, not the worst case. Third, mixing Hoare and Lomuto recursion boundaries. Fourth, claiming quick sort is stable. Fifth, forgetting that sorted input is the worst case for the last-element pivot.

What exams ask: 'Partition this array using Lomuto with the last element as pivot and show every step.' 'What is the worst case of quick sort and when does it happen?' 'Write the best and worst case recurrences and solve them.' 'Why is randomized quick sort expected O(n log n) on every input?' 'Compare quick sort and merge sort: time, space, stability.' Make a small table of the comparison; it is a favourite short question.

How to remember partition: Picture the array in four zones during Lomuto: small zone, big zone, not yet seen, and the pivot at the far end. Each step looks at the first unseen item and either leaves it in the big zone or swaps it to the end of the small zone. Draw these zones with a pencil on a row of boxes the first few times, and the code will feel natural.

Recap: Quick sort picks a pivot, partitions in linear time, and recurses on both sides with no combine. Lomuto is simple, Hoare does fewer swaps. Best and average case Theta(n log n), worst case Theta(n^2) when splits are lopsided. Random pivots make the expected time Theta(n log n) on every input. It is in-place but not stable. Next, we see more D&C tricks that speed up arithmetic and geometry.
key_points: Quick sort: partition around a pivot, recurse on both sides, no combine.
Lomuto: last element pivot, one scanning pointer; Hoare: two pointers moving inwards, fewer swaps.
Best and average case Theta(n log n); any constant-ratio split is enough.
Worst case Theta(n^2) when the pivot is always min or max, e.g. sorted input with last-element pivot.
Random pivot gives expected Theta(n log n) on every input (Las Vegas).
In-place with O(log n) stack if you recurse on the smaller side first; not stable.
Libraries use hybrids: introsort (quick + heap + insertion), median of three, three-way partition.
lessons.tip: Trace Lomuto partition on paper at least three times with different arrays. Once the four zones feel natural, quick sort questions become free marks.
lessons.task: Take 8 playing cards or 8 numbered paper slips. Shuffle them and quick sort them by hand using the last card as pivot, counting comparisons. Then sort them again starting from sorted order and compare the counts.

quiz.q: With the last element as pivot (Lomuto), which input causes the worst case?
quiz.explain: Each pivot is the maximum, so splits are n-1 and 0, giving Theta(n^2).

quiz.q: What is the expected running time of randomized quick sort on any input?
quiz.explain: Expectation is over the random pivot choices, so it holds for every input.

quiz.q: Which statement is true about quick sort?
options: Its worst case is Theta(n log n)
It is in-place but not stable
quiz.explain: Partition works inside the array, but long-distance swaps break stability.

quiz.explain: Depth is log base 10/9 of n and each level costs at most n.

lessons.title: More Divide and Conquer: Powers, Karatsuba, Strassen, Closest Pair
lessons.content:
Imagine you fold a sheet of paper in half, again and again. After 10 folds it is 1,024 layers thick. You did only 10 actions, but the result doubled 10 times. Divide and conquer has a similar magic for arithmetic: by splitting a big calculation into halves and reusing results cleverly, you can do in a few dozen steps what a simple loop does in millions. In this lesson we look at four famous examples: fast exponentiation, Karatsuba multiplication, Strassen's matrix multiplication and the closest pair of points.

The common pattern: All four algorithms follow the same plan. The obvious method has some cost. We split the input in half and write the answer in terms of the halves. Then we find a trick that needs fewer recursive calls than the obvious split, or we reuse one call's result. Fewer calls means a smaller a in T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n), and the master theorem turns that small change into a big speed-up.

Fast exponentiation, the slow way: To compute x^n, the simple loop multiplies x by itself n - 1 times. For n = 1,000,000 that is almost a million multiplications. Fine for a computer once, but cryptography does this with huge numbers thousands of times per second.

Fast exponentiation, the trick: Notice that x^n = (x^(n/2))^2 when n is even, and x^n = x times (x^((n-1)/2))^2 when n is odd. So power(x, n): if n == 0 return 1; h = power(x, n div 2); if n is even return h*h else return x*h*h. We compute the half power once and square it, instead of computing it twice. T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1), which is Theta(log n) multiplications.

Fast exponentiation, worked example: 3^13. 13 is odd, so 3^13 = 3 times (3^6)^2. 3^6 = (3^3)^2. 3^3 = 3 times (3^1)^2. 3^1 = 3 times (3^0)^2 = 3. Then 3^3 = 3 times 9 = 27, 3^6 = 729, 3^13 = 3 times 729^2 = 3 times 531,441 = 1,594,323. Only 5 multiplications instead of 12. For n = 1,000,000 it needs about 40 multiplications instead of 999,999. This is also called binary exponentiation, because it follows the binary digits of n.

Fast exponentiation without recursion: The same idea works as a loop. result = 1; while n > 0: if n is odd, result = result * x; x = x * x; n = n div 2. Each round looks at the last binary digit of n. For 13, which is 1101 in binary, the loop multiplies result by x^1, x^4 and x^8, since 1 + 4 + 8 = 13. For modular exponentiation, take mod m after every multiplication so numbers never grow too large. This loop version is what most real libraries use, because it avoids recursion overhead.

Where it is used: Modular exponentiation, computing x^n mod m, is the core of RSA and Diffie-Hellman, which protect online banking and messaging. With this method, numbers with hundreds of digits are handled in a fraction of a second. The same idea computes the n-th Fibonacci number in O(log n) matrix multiplications, by raising the matrix [[1, 1], [1, 0]] to the power n.

Karatsuba, the problem: Multiplying two n-digit numbers the school way multiplies every digit of one by every digit of the other: n^2 single-digit products. For two 1,000 digit numbers, that is a million digit products. Andrey Kolmogorov believed around 1960 that n^2 was the best possible. A 23 year old student, Anatoly Karatsuba, proved him wrong in 1960.

Karatsuba, the split: Write each number as two halves. With base 10 and m = n/2: x = a times 10^m + b, y = c times 10^m + d. Then xy = ac times 10^(2m) + (ad + bc) times 10^m + bd. That needs four half-size products: ac, ad, bc, bd. T(n) = 4T(n/2) + O(n), which by the master theorem is still Theta(n^2). No gain yet.

Karatsuba, the trick: Compute only three products: P1 = ac, P2 = bd, P3 = (a + b)(c + d). Then ad + bc = P3 - P1 - P2, because (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd. Additions and shifts are cheap, O(n). Now T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n), and log_2 3 is about 1.585, so Theta(n^1.585). For 1,000 digit numbers, roughly 57,000 digit products instead of a million.

Karatsuba, worked example: 12 times 34. a = 1, b = 2, c = 3, d = 4, m = 1. P1 = 1 times 3 = 3. P2 = 2 times 4 = 8. P3 = (1 + 2)(3 + 4) = 21. Middle = 21 - 3 - 8 = 10. Result = 3 times 100 + 10 times 10 + 8 = 300 + 100 + 8 = 408. Check: 12 times 34 = 408. Correct, with three small products instead of four.

Karatsuba, a bigger example: 1234 times 5678 with m = 2. a = 12, b = 34, c = 56, d = 78. P1 = 12 times 56 = 672. P2 = 34 times 78 = 2,652. P3 = (12 + 34)(56 + 78) = 46 times 134 = 6,164. Middle = 6,164 - 672 - 2,652 = 2,840. Result = 672 times 10,000 + 2,840 times 100 + 2,652 = 6,720,000 + 284,000 + 2,652 = 7,006,652. And indeed 1234 times 5678 = 7,006,652. In a real implementation the three smaller products would themselves be computed by Karatsuba, until the numbers are small enough for the school method.

Why additions are cheap but multiplications are not: Adding two n digit numbers takes Theta(n) digit operations, one pass with carries. Multiplying them the school way takes Theta(n^2). So trading one multiplication for several additions is a great deal when n is large. The same logic drives Strassen: adding two n by n matrices costs Theta(n^2), while multiplying them costs much more, so extra additions are worth it to save a multiplication.

Strassen, the problem: Multiplying two n by n matrices the normal way computes n^2 entries, each a sum of n products, so Theta(n^3). Splitting each matrix into four n/2 by n/2 blocks and multiplying blocks needs 8 block products: T(n) = 8T(n/2) + Theta(n^2) = Theta(n^3). Again, no gain from splitting alone.

Strassen, the trick: In 1969, Volker Strassen found a way to get the four result blocks using only 7 block multiplications, with 18 block additions and subtractions. You do not need to memorise all seven formulas for most exams, but know one: M1 = (A11 + A22)(B11 + B22), and the result blocks are sums and differences of M1 to M7. Now T(n) = 7T(n/2) + Theta(n^2), and log_2 7 is about 2.807, so Theta(n^2.81).

Strassen in practice: The constant factors are larger, it uses extra memory, and it is a bit less numerically stable with floating point numbers. So libraries use it only for big matrices, switching to the normal method below a cut-off size. Researchers have pushed the exponent lower, to around 2.37, but those algorithms are only of theoretical interest. The lesson is the idea: saving one multiplication at each level saves a lot overall.

Closest pair, the problem: Given n points on a plane, find the two points that are closest to each other. Checking all pairs takes Theta(n^2). With n = 100,000 points, that is about 5 billion distance calculations.

Closest pair, the D&C idea: Sort points by x. Split with a vertical line into a left half and a right half. Recursively find the closest distance dL on the left and dR on the right. Let d = min(dL, dR). The only pair that could be better is one point on each side, both within distance d of the dividing line. Collect points in that strip of width 2d, sorted by y.

Closest pair, the clever part: In the strip, each point only needs to be compared with a few points that follow it in y order, at most 7 by the usual packing argument, because points on the same side are at least d apart and only a small number fit in a d by 2d box. So the strip check is O(n). If points are kept sorted by y during the recursion, T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n log n). For 100,000 points, that is a few million steps instead of billions.

Real life example 1, online payment security: When you pay with bKash or a bank card online, your phone and the server set up a secure connection using public key cryptography such as RSA or Diffie-Hellman. These need numbers raised to huge powers modulo a big number. Without fast exponentiation, a single connection could take a long time. With repeated squaring, it takes milliseconds. Large number libraries also switch to Karatsuba when numbers get long enough.

Real life example 2, ships and air traffic: An air traffic control system over the Bay of Bengal must warn when two aircraft are too close. With thousands of flights, checking every pair again and again is wasteful. Closest pair style algorithms, or grids based on the same strip idea, quickly find the nearest pair and raise an alert. Game engines use similar tricks to detect which objects are close enough to collide.

Common mistakes: First, in fast exponentiation, calling power(x, n/2) twice and multiplying, which gives T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1 = Theta(n) and loses all the gain. Second, saying Karatsuba is O(n^1.5); the exponent is log_2 3, about 1.585. Third, saying Strassen is O(n^2); it is about n^2.81. Fourth, in closest pair, checking all points in the strip against each other, which can be quadratic.

What exams ask: 'Compute 2^10 or 3^13 by fast exponentiation and count multiplications.' 'Show Karatsuba on 1234 times 5678 for one level.' 'Write the recurrence for Strassen and solve it.' 'Explain why only a constant number of points in the strip need checking in closest pair.' Practising the small numeric examples is the quickest way to score.

Recap: Fast exponentiation computes a half power once and squares it, Theta(log n). Karatsuba replaces four half-size products with three, Theta(n^1.585). Strassen replaces eight block products with seven, Theta(n^2.81). Closest pair splits by a line and only checks a thin strip, O(n log n). One idea runs through all of them: reduce the number of recursive calls, and the master theorem rewards you. Before you move on, try writing the recurrence for each of the four algorithms from memory and solving it, because that is exactly what most exam questions on this topic look like.

Looking ahead: Divide and conquer also appears in the Fast Fourier Transform, which multiplies polynomials in O(n log n) and powers audio processing and very fast big number multiplication. You will meet it in signal processing or advanced algorithms courses. For now, remember that a smart combine or a saved recursive call can change the exponent of your running time.
key_points: Trick of this lesson: reduce the number of recursive calls, and the master theorem lowers the exponent.
Fast exponentiation: compute x^(n/2) once and square it; Theta(log n) multiplications.
Modular exponentiation powers RSA and Diffie-Hellman; matrix power gives Fibonacci in O(log n).
Karatsuba: 3 products instead of 4, Theta(n^log2 3) about n^1.585.
Strassen: 7 block products instead of 8, Theta(n^log2 7) about n^2.81; used only for large matrices.
Closest pair: split by a vertical line, check a strip of width 2d with a constant number of neighbours, O(n log n).
Calling the half problem twice instead of once destroys the speed-up.
lessons.tip: When you see a D&C recurrence, ask: can I save one recursive call? That single question explains Karatsuba, Strassen and fast power.

lessons.title: Sorting Lower Bound and Linear-Time Sorts
lessons.content:
Imagine playing a guessing game with your cousin. She thinks of one of 8 animals, and you may only ask yes or no questions. With clever questions like 'is it in the first half of the list?', you need 3 questions, because 2^3 = 8. No matter how smart you are, you can never guarantee fewer than 3, because each answer only splits the possibilities into two groups. Sorting by comparisons is the same game, just with many more possibilities. This lesson proves that any comparison sort needs about n log n comparisons, and then shows how sorts that do not compare can beat that limit.

Comparison sorts: A comparison sort learns about the order of the input only by comparing pairs of elements: is A[i] < A[j]? Insertion sort, merge sort, quick sort and heap sort are all comparison sorts. They never look at the digits or bits of a key; they only ask which of two keys is smaller. This is useful because it works for any data you can compare, like names, dates or prices.

The decision tree model: Any comparison sort, run on inputs of size n, can be drawn as a binary tree. Each internal node is a comparison 'a_i <= a_j?'. The left child is what the algorithm does if the answer is yes, the right child if no. Each leaf is a final answer: a permutation saying how to rearrange the input into sorted order. Running the algorithm on one input means following one path from root to leaf. The number of comparisons in the worst case equals the height of the tree.

A tiny decision tree: For three elements a, b, c, there are 3! = 6 possible orders. One tree: compare a and b. If a <= b, compare b and c; if b <= c the answer is a, b, c; otherwise compare a and c to decide between a, c, b and c, a, b. The other side is symmetric. This tree has 6 leaves and height 3, so sorting 3 elements needs 3 comparisons in the worst case. You cannot do it with 2, because a tree of height 2 has at most 4 leaves, fewer than 6.

The lower bound argument: A correct sort must be able to output every one of the n! permutations, because each could be the right answer for some input. So the decision tree needs at least n! leaves. A binary tree of height h has at most 2^h leaves. So 2^h >= n!, which means h >= log2(n!). That is the minimum worst case number of comparisons for any comparison sort.

How big is log2(n!): log2(n!) = log2(1) + log2(2) + ... + log2(n). The upper half of these terms, from n/2 to n, are each at least log2(n/2), and there are n/2 of them. So log2(n!) >= (n/2) log2(n/2), which is Omega(n log n). Stirling's formula gives the precise value, about n log2 n - 1.44n. Conclusion: every comparison sort needs Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Merge sort and heap sort reach this, so they are asymptotically optimal comparison sorts.

What the bound does not say: It is about comparisons in the worst case, and the same argument also holds for the average case. It does not say that every algorithm needs n log n time. If an algorithm uses other information, such as the actual value of a key as an array index, it is not in the decision tree model, and it can be faster. That is the door to linear time sorting.

Counting sort, the idea: Suppose all keys are integers between 0 and k. Instead of comparing, count how many times each value appears. Then compute running totals so you know, for each value, how many keys are less than or equal to it. That total is exactly the final position of that value. Finally, place each element into its position.

Counting sort, step by step: Input A = [2, 5, 3, 0, 2, 3, 0, 3], k = 5. Count C[0..5] = [2, 0, 2, 3, 0, 1]. Prefix sums: C = [2, 2, 4, 7, 7, 8]. Now scan A from right to left. A[7] = 3: C[3] = 7, put 3 at position 7 (1-based), C[3] = 6. A[6] = 0: put at position 2, C[0] = 1. And so on. The output is [0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 5].

Counting sort in pseudo-code: countingSort(A, k): C = array of k + 1 zeros. For each x in A: C[x] = C[x] + 1. For v from 1 to k: C[v] = C[v] + C[v - 1]. For i from n down to 1: B[C[A[i]]] = A[i]; C[A[i]] = C[A[i]] - 1. Return B. Notice that there is no 'if A[i] < A[j]' anywhere. The values themselves are used as addresses in the array C. That single fact is why the decision tree argument does not apply. In real programs we usually sort records, not bare numbers, for example students by marks, and the same code moves the whole record into B.

Counting sort, analysis and stability: Counting takes Theta(n), prefix sums Theta(k), placing Theta(n). Total Theta(n + k), with Theta(n + k) extra space. If k is O(n), that is linear time. Scanning from right to left makes it stable: equal keys keep their original order. Stability is not just nice here, it is essential for radix sort. The weakness: if k is huge, like sorting 10 numbers up to one billion, the count array is enormous and the method is useless.

Radix sort, the idea: Sort numbers digit by digit, starting from the least significant digit, using a stable sort, usually counting sort, for each digit. After sorting by the units digit, then by the tens digit, then by the hundreds digit, the whole list is sorted. This is how old punched card sorting machines worked, one column at a time.

Radix sort, worked example: [329, 457, 657, 839, 436, 720, 355]. Sort by units digit: [720, 355, 436, 457, 657, 329, 839]. Sort by tens digit, stably: [720, 329, 436, 839, 355, 457, 657]. Sort by hundreds digit, stably: [329, 355, 436, 457, 657, 720, 839]. Done. Notice that 329 and 355 were already in the right order from the tens pass, and the stable hundreds pass kept them that way. That is why stability is essential.

Radix sort, analysis: With d digits, each in base b, and counting sort per digit, time is Theta(d(n + b)). For 32-bit integers, we can treat each number as 4 digits of 8 bits, so b = 256 and d = 4: time Theta(4(n + 256)), which is linear in n. If d is constant and b is O(n), radix sort is linear. It does not break the lower bound; it simply is not a comparison sort.

Bucket sort, the idea: Suppose keys are real numbers spread uniformly over [0, 1). Make n buckets, each covering an interval of width 1/n. Put each key x into bucket floor(n times x). Sort each bucket with insertion sort, then join the buckets in order. Example with n = 5: 0.78 goes to bucket 3, 0.17 to bucket 0, 0.39 to bucket 1, 0.26 to bucket 1, 0.72 to bucket 3. Sort buckets: [0.17], [0.26, 0.39], [], [0.72, 0.78], []. Join: 0.17, 0.26, 0.39, 0.72, 0.78.

Bucket sort, analysis: If keys are uniformly distributed, each bucket gets about one key on average, and the expected total time is Theta(n). The proof uses the fact that the expected value of the square of a bucket size is less than 2. But if the data is not uniform, for example all keys between 0.50 and 0.51, everything lands in one bucket and the insertion sort makes it Theta(n^2). Bucket sort is an average-case algorithm that depends on the input distribution.

Choosing among linear sorts: Counting sort is best for small integer ranges, like exam marks from 0 to 100. Radix sort is great for fixed-length keys like IDs, phone numbers or dates. Bucket sort suits uniformly spread real numbers. All three trade generality for speed: they need extra knowledge about the keys, while comparison sorts work on anything comparable.

Real life example 1, SSC marks: An education board wants to sort 2 million students by total marks between 0 and 1,300. Counting sort uses an array of 1,301 counters. One pass counts, one pass computes prefix sums, one pass places students. About 4 million simple steps, no comparisons, and it is stable, so students with equal marks stay in, say, roll number order. A comparison sort would need around 2 million times 21, about 42 million comparisons.

Real life example 2, sorting mobile numbers: A telecom company sorts 50 million Bangladeshi mobile numbers of 11 digits like 01712345678. Radix sort processes them digit by digit, or 2 or 3 digits at a time, with a stable counting sort on each pass. The number of passes is fixed by the length of the number, not by how many customers there are, so the total work grows linearly with the number of customers.

Common mistakes: First, saying 'no sorting algorithm can beat n log n'. Correct is 'no comparison sort'. Second, using an unstable sort inside radix sort, which gives wrong results. Third, running radix sort from the most significant digit with the simple method, which does not work without extra care. Fourth, forgetting the + k in counting sort's Theta(n + k). Fifth, claiming bucket sort is always linear.

What exams ask: 'Prove that any comparison sort needs Omega(n log n) comparisons using decision trees.' 'Draw the decision tree for insertion sort on 3 elements.' 'Show counting sort on this array with the C array after each step.' 'Show radix sort on these numbers pass by pass.' 'When is bucket sort linear, and when does it fail?' The proof question is very common, so practise writing it in five lines.

A five line proof to memorise: One, model the algorithm as a decision tree. Two, it must have at least n! leaves, one for each possible permutation. Three, a binary tree of height h has at most 2^h leaves. Four, so h >= log2(n!). Five, log2(n!) = Theta(n log n), so the worst case needs Omega(n log n) comparisons.

Recap: Comparison sorts can be modelled as decision trees with at least n! leaves, so they need Omega(n log n) comparisons; merge sort and heap sort are optimal. Counting sort runs in Theta(n + k) for small integer keys and is stable. Radix sort applies a stable sort digit by digit in Theta(d(n + b)). Bucket sort is Theta(n) on average for uniform data. Next lesson, we find the k-th smallest element without fully sorting. Keep the decision tree picture in mind; we will use similar counting arguments later when we talk about the limits of algorithms and NP-completeness.
key_points: A comparison sort only learns order by comparing pairs; it can be drawn as a decision tree.
The tree needs at least n! leaves and a height-h binary tree has at most 2^h leaves, so h >= log2(n!) = Omega(n log n).
Merge sort and heap sort are asymptotically optimal comparison sorts.
Counting sort: Theta(n + k) for integer keys in 0..k, stable if placed right to left.
Radix sort: stable sort by least significant digit first; Theta(d(n + b)).
Bucket sort: expected Theta(n) for uniform keys in [0,1), Theta(n^2) worst case.
Linear sorts do not break the lower bound; they are not comparison sorts.
lessons.tip: Before choosing a sort, ask what you know about the keys. Small integer range? Counting sort. Fixed length? Radix. Unknown? A good comparison sort.
lessons.task: Write the last 3 digits of 8 friends' phone numbers on paper slips. Radix sort them by hand: units digit, then tens, then hundreds, keeping equal digits in the same order each pass. Check the final order.

When most keys fall into the same bucket
