Which statement about backtracking is true?
options: It always runs in polynomial time
It is still exponential in the worst case but prunes many branches in practice
It never needs to undo choices
quiz.explain: Pruning helps a lot, but NP-hard problems remain hard in the worst case.

lessons.title: String Matching: Naive, Rabin-Karp, KMP
lessons.content:
Imagine pressing Ctrl+F in a long PDF of the Bangladesh constitution and typing 'citizen'. In a blink, every occurrence is highlighted. Behind that blink is a string matching algorithm. The simple way would compare the word at every position, which is fine for a page but slow for a whole library or a DNA sequence with billions of letters. In this lesson we study the naive method, the Rabin-Karp rolling hash, and the Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) algorithm with its prefix function, and compare their running times.

The problem: We have a text T of length n and a pattern P of length m, with m <= n, over some alphabet, such as English letters, Bangla letters, digits or the DNA letters A, C, G, T. We want every shift s, from 0 to n - m, such that T[s+1 .. s+m] = P[1 .. m]. Each such s is a valid shift, or an occurrence of P in T.

The naive algorithm: For every shift s from 0 to n - m, compare P with the text window starting at s, character by character, and stop at the first mismatch. In code: for s from 0 to n - m: j = 0; while j < m and T[s + j] == P[j]: j = j + 1; if j == m: report s. Simple and correct.

Naive, the analysis: There are n - m + 1 shifts and each can take up to m comparisons, so the worst case is O((n - m + 1) m), which is O(nm). The bad case: T = AAAA...A (n letters) and P = AAA...AB (m letters). At every shift, m - 1 characters match before the B fails. On random English text, mismatches usually come quickly and the naive method is fast in practice, but we want a guarantee.

The waste in the naive method: When a window fails after matching many characters, the naive method moves one step and forgets everything it learned. If P = ABABC and we matched ABAB before failing, we already know the text there is ABAB. Both KMP and Rabin-Karp avoid this waste, in very different ways: Rabin-Karp turns comparison into cheap arithmetic, while KMP remembers what has been matched.

Rabin-Karp, the idea: Treat each m-character string as a number, compute a hash of the pattern, and compare it with the hash of each text window. If hashes differ, the strings certainly differ. If hashes match, check the characters to be sure. The trick that makes it fast is a rolling hash: the hash of the next window is computed from the previous one in O(1) time.

The rolling hash: With digits as the alphabet and base d = 10, a window like 314 is the number 314. Sliding to the next window, 141, means: remove the leading digit's contribution, shift left, and add the new digit: 141 = (314 - 3 times 100) times 10 + 1. To keep numbers small, do everything modulo a prime q: t_(s+1) = (d (t_s - T[s+1] h) + T[s+m+1]) mod q, where h = d^(m-1) mod q. For letters, use d = alphabet size, like 256.

Rabin-Karp worked example: Text 3141592653589, pattern 26, q = 11. Hash of the pattern: 26 mod 11 = 4. Window hashes: 31 gives 9, 14 gives 3, 41 gives 8, 15 gives 4, 59 gives 4, 92 gives 4, 26 gives 4, 65 gives 10, and so on. Hash matches occur at windows 15, 59, 92 and 26. Character checks reject 15, 59 and 92; these are spurious hits. Only 26, at shift 6, is a real match. Rolling check: from 31 (hash 9) to 14: ((9 - 3 times 10) times 10 + 4) mod 11 = (-206) mod 11 = 3. Correct.

Rabin-Karp, the analysis: Preprocessing the pattern hash and h is O(m). Each window hash is O(1) by rolling, so scanning is O(n) plus the cost of character checks. With a good large prime, spurious hits are rare, and the expected time is O(n + m). In the worst case, if every window is a hash hit (for example many true matches or a bad q), each check costs O(m), giving O(nm). Choosing q as a large random prime makes bad cases very unlikely.

Where Rabin-Karp shines: It extends easily to searching for many patterns at once: put all pattern hashes in a hash set, and check each window's hash against the set. Plagiarism detectors use this idea, hashing every k-word chunk of a document and looking for chunks shared with other documents. It also extends to two-dimensional pattern search in images.

KMP, the idea: Knuth, Morris and Pratt (1977) found a way to never move backwards in the text. When a mismatch happens after matching q characters of P, the algorithm already knows those q text characters, because they equal P[1..q]. So it can compute, from the pattern alone, how far the pattern can safely slide. This information is stored in the prefix function.

The prefix function: For each position q of the pattern, pi[q] is the length of the longest proper prefix of P[1..q] that is also a suffix of P[1..q]. Proper means not the whole string. Example: P = ABABACA. For q = 5, P[1..5] = ABABA; the prefix ABA is also a suffix, and no longer proper prefix works, so pi[5] = 3. The full table is pi = [0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1].

Computing the prefix function: k = 0; pi[1] = 0. For q from 2 to m: while k > 0 and P[k+1] != P[q]: k = pi[k]. If P[k+1] == P[q]: k = k + 1. pi[q] = k. The while loop falls back through shorter borders. Although it looks like it could be slow, an amortized argument (lesson 11) shows the total work is O(m): k increases at most m times, and each fall back decreases it, so it cannot decrease more than it increased.

The KMP matcher: q = 0 (number of characters matched). For i from 1 to n: while q > 0 and P[q+1] != T[i]: q = pi[q]. If P[q+1] == T[i]: q = q + 1. If q == m: report a match at shift i - m; q = pi[q] to keep looking for overlapping matches. The text index i only moves forward. By the same amortized argument, the matcher is O(n), so KMP is O(n + m) in the worst case, not just on average.

KMP worked example: Text ABABABACA, pattern ABABACA, pi = [0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1]. Match A, B, A, B, A: q = 5. Next text char is B, but P[6] = C, mismatch. Fall back q = pi[5] = 3, meaning ABA is still matched. P[4] = B matches the text B: q = 4. Then A: q = 5. C: q = 6. A: q = 7 = m, match found at shift 2. The naive method would have restarted at shift 1 and re-read characters; KMP never re-reads the text.

Another prefix function to practise: For P = AABAAB, pi = [0, 1, 0, 1, 2, 3]. For P = ABABCABAB, pi = [0, 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4]. Check one: for q = 9, ABABCABAB, the prefix ABAB equals the suffix ABAB, length 4. Being fluent with this table is the key to every KMP exam question.

The finite automaton view: CLRS also presents a string matching automaton. For a pattern of length m, build a machine with states 0 to m, where state q means 'the last q text characters match the first q pattern characters'. For each state and each alphabet letter, precompute the next state. Then the text is scanned with exactly one table lookup per character, O(n) matching time. The catch is preprocessing: the table has (m + 1) times the alphabet size entries, which is expensive for large alphabets like Unicode. KMP can be seen as a clever way to get the same effect while storing only the m values of pi and computing transitions on the fly.

Comparison of the three: Naive: no preprocessing, O(nm) worst case, simple and fine for short patterns. Rabin-Karp: O(m) preprocessing, O(n + m) expected and O(nm) worst case, great for multiple patterns. KMP: O(m) preprocessing, O(n + m) worst case, never backs up in the text, ideal for streaming data. In practice, tools like grep use variants such as Boyer-Moore, which skips ahead using the last characters of the pattern and is often sublinear on normal text.

Real life example 1, searching Bangla text: A Bangla news site lets readers search old articles for a phrase. Bangla text in Unicode uses several code points per visible letter, so patterns can be long in code units. KMP's guarantee of O(n + m) with no backtracking over the text is useful when articles are streamed from storage. Search engines, of course, build indexes in advance, but string matching is still used to highlight the matched phrase inside each result.

Real life example 2, DNA and virus detection: Researchers studying dengue or COVID-19 samples in Bangladesh search long genome sequences, strings over A, C, G, T, for known marker patterns. With a genome of 30,000 letters and hundreds of markers, a Rabin-Karp style multi-pattern search or its relative, the Aho-Corasick automaton, finds all markers in one pass. Antivirus programs use the same idea to scan files for many virus signatures at once.

Common mistakes: First, in Rabin-Karp, forgetting to verify characters on a hash match, which reports spurious hits as real matches. Second, getting a negative number after subtraction in the rolling formula; add q before taking mod. Third, in the prefix function, including the whole string as a prefix; it must be a proper prefix. Fourth, after a full KMP match, resetting q to 0 instead of pi[m], which misses overlapping matches like finding AA in AAAA.

What exams ask: 'Compute the prefix function for ABABACA.' 'Run KMP on this text and pattern, showing q after each character.' 'Show the Rabin-Karp hashes for this text with q = 11 or 13, and point out spurious hits.' 'Give the worst case of the naive algorithm and an input that causes it.' 'Compare the three algorithms.' A small table with columns i, T[i], q is the clearest way to show KMP.

Recap: String matching finds all shifts where P occurs in T. Naive checks every shift, O(nm) worst case. Rabin-Karp compares rolling hashes mod a prime and verifies on hits, O(n + m) expected, O(nm) worst. KMP precomputes the prefix function pi in O(m) and scans the text once without backing up, O(n + m) worst case, thanks to an amortized argument. Next: P, NP and NP-completeness, where we ask which problems have fast algorithms at all.
key_points: String matching finds every shift s where pattern P (length m) occurs in text T (length n).
Naive: check every shift; O(nm) worst case, e.g. T = AAAA...A, P = AA...AB.
Rabin-Karp: rolling hash mod a prime q; verify characters on hash hits; O(n + m) expected, O(nm) worst.
Rolling update: t_(s+1) = (d (t_s - T[s+1] h) + T[s+m+1]) mod q with h = d^(m-1) mod q.
Prefix function pi[q] = longest proper prefix of P[1..q] that is also its suffix; computed in O(m).
KMP never moves back in the text: O(n + m) worst case; after a match set q = pi[m].
Rabin-Karp suits many patterns at once; KMP suits streaming; Boyer-Moore is often fastest in practice.
lessons.tip: Practise the prefix function on five different patterns until you can write it in under a minute. Almost every KMP question starts with that table.
lessons.task: Write the prefix function for your own name in capital English letters (for example ANANYA or RAHIM). Then write a 20-letter text containing your name twice and run KMP by hand, recording q after each letter.

quiz.explain: Up to m comparisons at each of n - m + 1 shifts.

A pattern longer than the text
quiz.explain: Equal hashes do not guarantee equal strings; characters must be checked.

quiz.q: What is the prefix function of ABABACA?
quiz.explain: For example pi[5] = 3 because ABA is both a prefix and a suffix of ABABA.

quiz.q: What is the worst-case time of KMP?
quiz.explain: Prefix function O(m) and matcher O(n) by an amortized argument.

quiz.explain: Resetting to pi[m] keeps the longest border so overlapping occurrences are found.

lessons.title: P, NP and NP-Completeness
lessons.content:
Imagine your friend gives you a finished Sudoku and asks, 'Is this correct?' You check every row, column and box in a minute. Now imagine she gives you an empty, very large Sudoku and asks you to solve it. That can take hours, or for giant puzzles, longer than a lifetime. Checking an answer is easy; finding one seems hard. This gap between checking and finding is the heart of the most famous open question in computer science: is P equal to NP? In this lesson we learn what P and NP mean, what reductions are, why SAT is special, the classic NP-complete problems, and what NP-hard means.

Tractable and intractable: So far, almost every algorithm in this course ran in polynomial time: O(n), O(n log n), O(n^3). We call problems with polynomial-time algorithms tractable. For some problems, like 0/1 knapsack with large weights, travelling salesman and graph colouring, we only know exponential algorithms. With n = 100, an algorithm needing 2^n steps would run far longer than the age of the universe, even on a computer doing a billion steps per second: about 40 trillion years. Such problems are called intractable in practice.

Decision problems: To build a clean theory, we mostly study decision problems, whose answer is yes or no. Instead of 'find the shortest tour', ask 'is there a tour of length at most k?'. Instead of 'colour this graph with the fewest colours', ask 'can it be coloured with 3 colours?'. This is not a big loss: if we can answer the decision version quickly, we can usually find the optimal value by binary search on k, and often the solution itself.

The class P: P is the set of decision problems that can be solved by an algorithm in polynomial time, O(n^c) for some constant c, where n is the input size in bits. Examples: is there a path from s to t? (BFS). Is this array sorted? Is the shortest path from s to t at most k? (Dijkstra). Does this graph have a perfect matching? (max flow). Is this number prime? (yes, the AKS algorithm, 2002, put primality in P).

The class NP: NP is the set of decision problems where, whenever the answer is yes, there is a short proof, called a certificate, that can be checked in polynomial time. For 'is there a tour of length at most k?', the certificate is the tour itself; checking it means verifying it visits every city once and adding up its length. For 'can this graph be 3-coloured?', the certificate is the colouring; checking means looking at every edge. NP stands for nondeterministic polynomial time, not 'not polynomial'.

P is inside NP: Every problem in P is also in NP. If you can solve it in polynomial time, you can verify a yes answer by simply solving it again, ignoring the certificate. So P is a subset of NP. The big open question is whether NP contains problems that are not in P. Most researchers believe P is not equal to NP, but nobody has proved it. The Clay Mathematics Institute offers one million US dollars for a proof either way.

Why P versus NP matters: If P = NP, then every problem whose solution can be checked quickly could also be solved quickly. Many cryptographic systems used for online banking, such as RSA, rely on certain problems being hard to solve but easy to check. Proving P = NP with a practical algorithm would change cryptography, scheduling, logistics and more. Proving P is not NP would confirm that some problems are inherently hard.

Reductions: A reduction transforms one problem into another. We say A reduces to B in polynomial time, written A <=p B, if there is a polynomial-time function f that turns any instance x of A into an instance f(x) of B, such that x is a yes instance of A exactly when f(x) is a yes instance of B. Then, if B can be solved quickly, so can A: transform and solve. In words, A is no harder than B.

A simple reduction example: Bipartite matching reduces to max flow, as in lesson 22: build the flow network from the bipartite graph; a matching of size k exists if and only if the max flow is at least k. Another: Hamiltonian cycle reduces to TSP: given a graph, make a complete graph where original edges cost 1 and missing edges cost 2; there is a Hamiltonian cycle if and only if there is a tour of cost exactly n.

NP-hard and NP-complete: A problem B is NP-hard if every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time. It is at least as hard as anything in NP. A problem is NP-complete if it is NP-hard and also in NP. NP-complete problems are the hardest problems in NP. If any single NP-complete problem had a polynomial algorithm, then every NP problem would, and P would equal NP.

The first NP-complete problem, SAT: The satisfiability problem SAT asks: given a Boolean formula with variables x1, x2, ... and operators AND, OR, NOT, is there an assignment of true and false that makes the whole formula true? Example: (x1 OR NOT x2) AND (x2 OR x3) AND (NOT x1 OR NOT x3). Try x1 = true, x2 = true, x3 = false: first clause true, second true, third true. Satisfiable.

Cook-Levin theorem: In 1971, Stephen Cook, and independently Leonid Levin, proved that SAT is NP-complete. The idea: any NP problem has a polynomial-time verifier, which is a machine running for polynomially many steps. One can write a large but polynomial-size Boolean formula that is satisfiable exactly when some certificate makes the verifier accept. This was the seed. After that, proving a new problem NP-complete only needs a reduction from a known NP-complete problem.

3-SAT: 3-SAT restricts SAT to formulas in conjunctive normal form with exactly three literals per clause. It is still NP-complete, and it is the favourite starting point for reductions because its structure is simple. Interestingly, 2-SAT, with two literals per clause, is in P and can be solved in linear time with strongly connected components, the Kosaraju idea from lesson 18.

The recipe for proving NP-completeness: To prove a new problem X is NP-complete: Step 1, show X is in NP by describing a certificate and a polynomial-time verifier. Step 2, pick a known NP-complete problem Y. Step 3, give a polynomial-time reduction from Y to X: transform any instance of Y into an instance of X. Step 4, prove both directions: yes for Y implies yes for X, and yes for X implies yes for Y. Direction matters: reduce from the known hard problem to the new one, never the other way.

Classic NP-complete problems: Richard Karp showed in 1972 that 21 natural problems are NP-complete. The most commonly taught: SAT and 3-SAT; CLIQUE (does the graph have k vertices all connected to each other?); INDEPENDENT SET (k vertices with no edges between them); VERTEX COVER (k vertices touching every edge); HAMILTONIAN CYCLE (a cycle visiting every vertex once); TSP decision version; SUBSET SUM; 0/1 KNAPSACK decision version; GRAPH 3-COLOURING; and SET COVER.

A neat chain of reductions: 3-SAT reduces to CLIQUE: for each clause make a group of three vertices for its literals, connect vertices from different groups unless they are contradictory, like x and NOT x; the formula is satisfiable if and only if there is a clique of size equal to the number of clauses. CLIQUE reduces to INDEPENDENT SET by taking the complement graph. INDEPENDENT SET of size k exists if and only if VERTEX COVER of size n - k exists, since the vertices outside an independent set cover every edge.

NP-hard beyond NP: Some problems are NP-hard but not in NP, usually because they are not decision problems or their yes answers have no short certificate. The optimisation version of TSP, 'find the shortest tour', is NP-hard. The halting problem is NP-hard too, and it is not even solvable at all. So NP-hard means 'at least as hard as NP', with no upper limit.

What to do with an NP-hard problem: Do not give up; change the question. Use exact exponential methods for small inputs, like backtracking or branch and bound (lesson 23) or DP with pseudo-polynomial time (lesson 15). Use approximation algorithms with a guaranteed ratio (lesson 26). Use heuristics like local search or genetic algorithms that work well in practice without guarantees. Or look for special cases in P, such as TSP on very small graphs, knapsack with small capacity, or 2-SAT.

Real life example 1, the exam routine problem: A university with 500 courses wants an exam routine in 10 days with no student having two exams on one day. This is graph colouring, NP-complete in general. The exam office does not need a perfect theory; it uses heuristics like 'schedule the most conflicting course first' and accepts a good routine. Knowing the problem is NP-complete saves the IT team from searching forever for a fast exact algorithm that probably does not exist.

Real life example 2, delivery routing: Daraz, Foodpanda and courier companies plan routes for thousands of deliveries daily. Their core problem is a version of TSP and vehicle routing, both NP-hard. They use approximation and smart heuristics, combined with exact solvers for small parts of the problem. The theory of NP-completeness tells engineers which parts are fundamentally hard and where to focus clever tricks.

Common mistakes: First, thinking NP means 'not polynomial'; it means nondeterministic polynomial, and P is inside NP. Second, reducing in the wrong direction: to show X is hard, reduce a known hard problem to X. Third, forgetting to show the problem is in NP when proving NP-completeness. Fourth, saying NP-complete problems can never be solved; they can, just not known to be solvable in polynomial time. Fifth, calling knapsack's O(nW) a polynomial algorithm, which would wrongly imply P = NP.

What exams ask: 'Define P, NP, NP-hard and NP-complete with examples.' 'Draw the relationship between P, NP, NP-complete and NP-hard assuming P is not NP.' 'State the Cook-Levin theorem.' 'Show that vertex cover is in NP.' 'Reduce independent set to vertex cover.' 'Why does a polynomial algorithm for one NP-complete problem imply P = NP?' A clear Venn diagram and a careful statement of reduction direction earn most marks.

The picture to remember: Assuming P is not NP, draw a big oval NP. Inside it, a smaller region P on one side. On the other edge of NP, the NP-complete problems. A larger region NP-hard overlaps NP exactly at NP-complete and extends outside NP. If P = NP, the picture collapses: P, NP and NP-complete become the same set, apart from trivial problems.

Recap: P contains decision problems solvable in polynomial time; NP contains those whose yes answers can be verified in polynomial time with a certificate; P is a subset of NP, and whether they are equal is open. A reduction A <=p B shows A is no harder than B. NP-hard means every NP problem reduces to it; NP-complete means NP-hard and in NP. SAT was the first NP-complete problem (Cook-Levin), followed by 3-SAT, CLIQUE, vertex cover, Hamiltonian cycle, TSP, subset sum, knapsack and 3-colouring. Next: approximation and randomized algorithms, and a wrap-up of the course.

lessons.title: Approximation and Randomized Algorithms, and Course Wrap-up
lessons.content:
Imagine a cricket coach who has ten minutes to pick a batting order. The perfect order might take days to compute, but he knows a simple rule that is never worse than twice the ideal. He uses it and wins the match. Or imagine a teacher who checks a huge pile of homework by picking a random sample of pages instead of reading everything. Both are wise trade-offs: good enough answers fast, or correct answers with a little help from luck. This final lesson covers approximation algorithms, randomized algorithms, and then wraps up the whole course with a cheat-sheet of paradigms and what to learn next.

Why approximation: Lesson 25 showed that many important optimisation problems are NP-hard, so we probably cannot solve them exactly in polynomial time. An approximation algorithm runs in polynomial time and returns a solution that is provably close to optimal. Not a guess, a guarantee.

The approximation ratio: For a minimisation problem, an algorithm has ratio rho if, for every input, its cost C satisfies C <= rho times C*, where C* is the optimal cost. For maximisation, C >= C* / rho. A 2-approximation for a minimisation problem never returns more than twice the optimal cost. The proof usually compares the algorithm's answer with a lower bound on C*, because C* itself is unknown.

Vertex cover, the problem: In a graph, a vertex cover is a set of vertices touching every edge. Finding the smallest one is NP-hard. Think of placing security guards at corridor junctions so that every corridor is watched from at least one end.

Vertex cover, the 2-approximation: C = empty. While there are uncovered edges: pick any uncovered edge (u, v), add both u and v to C, and remove all edges touching u or v. Return C. Time O(V + E). Simple, almost silly, and yet provably good.

Why it is a 2-approximation: Let A be the set of edges the algorithm picked. No two edges in A share a vertex, because after picking (u, v) we remove all edges touching them. So A is a matching. Any vertex cover, including the optimal one, must contain at least one endpoint of each edge in A, and since these edges are disjoint, different edges need different vertices. So C* >= |A|. The algorithm adds 2 vertices per edge: |C| = 2|A| <= 2 C*. The lower bound used is the size of a matching.

Vertex cover example: A path a, b, c, d, e with edges a-b, b-c, c-d, d-e. Optimal cover: {b, d}, size 2. The algorithm might pick edge b-c, add b and c, removing a-b, b-c and c-d; then pick d-e, add d and e. Cover {b, c, d, e}, size 4, exactly 2 times the optimum, matching the bound. A natural greedy idea, 'pick the vertex with the highest degree', sounds smarter but has no constant ratio; its worst case grows like log n.

Metric TSP, the setting: In TSP with the triangle inequality, the direct road is never longer than a detour: w(a, c) <= w(a, b) + w(b, c). Real road distances roughly satisfy this. General TSP cannot be approximated within any constant unless P = NP, but metric TSP can.

Metric TSP, the 2-approximation idea: Step 1, compute a minimum spanning tree T (lesson 19). Step 2, walk around the tree, a full DFS walk that goes down and back up every edge, which costs exactly 2 w(T). Step 3, shortcut: list cities in the order they are first visited in the walk, skipping repeats, and return to the start. Shortcuts never increase length because of the triangle inequality.

Why it is within 2: Removing any one edge from an optimal tour leaves a spanning path, which is a spanning tree, so w(T) <= C*. The full walk costs 2 w(T) <= 2 C*, and shortcutting only makes it shorter. So the tour is at most twice the optimum. Christofides' algorithm improves the ratio to 1.5 by adding a minimum-weight perfect matching on the odd-degree vertices of T. For exams, the MST-based 2-approximation is the standard one to explain.

Metric TSP worked example: Four towns A, B, C, D on a straight road at kilometre marks 0, 1, 2 and 3, so distances are just differences. An MST is the chain A-B, B-C, C-D with weight 3. The full walk from A is A, B, C, D, C, B, A with length 6. Shortcutting repeated towns gives the tour A, B, C, D, A with length 1 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 6. The optimal tour also has length 6, since any tour must go out to D and come back. Here the approximation happens to be optimal; the guarantee only promises at most twice the optimum, and on other inputs the gap can be larger.

Other approximation ideas briefly: Greedy set cover achieves ratio about ln n. Knapsack has a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS): for any epsilon, a solution within (1 - epsilon) of optimal in time polynomial in n and 1/epsilon, by rounding values and using DP. These show that NP-hard problems differ a lot in how well they can be approximated.

Randomized algorithms: A randomized algorithm makes random choices during its run, like flipping coins. The randomness is in the algorithm, not in the input, so the guarantees hold for every input. We already met randomized quick sort (lesson 7), randomized select (lesson 10) and Rabin-Karp with a random prime (lesson 24).

Las Vegas algorithms: A Las Vegas algorithm always gives the correct answer, but its running time is random. Randomized quick sort is the classic example: the output is always sorted, and the expected time is O(n log n), although an unlucky run could take O(n^2). Quickselect is another. You can think: 'the result is guaranteed, the time is a gamble with very good odds'.

Monte Carlo algorithms: A Monte Carlo algorithm always runs within a fixed time bound, but its answer may be wrong with some small probability. Example: the Miller-Rabin primality test. For a number n, pick a random base and do a quick check. If n is prime, it always says 'probably prime'. If n is composite, each round wrongly says 'probably prime' with probability at most 1/4. After 20 independent rounds, the error probability is at most (1/4)^20, less than one in a trillion. Cryptography libraries use this to find large primes for RSA.

Another Monte Carlo example, Freivalds' check: Given three n by n matrices A, B and C, is AB = C? Computing AB costs O(n^3). Freivalds picks a random 0/1 vector r and checks whether A(Br) = Cr, which needs only three matrix-vector products, O(n^2). If AB = C, the test always passes. If not, it fails with probability at least 1/2. Repeat k times to make the error at most 1/2^k. Fast checking of a slow computation.

Karger's randomized min cut: Another famous Monte Carlo algorithm finds a minimum cut of an undirected graph by repeatedly picking a random edge and contracting it, merging its two endpoints, until only two super-vertices remain. The edges between them form a cut. A single run finds a minimum cut with probability at least 2/(n(n - 1)), which is small, but repeating it about n^2 log n times makes failure very unlikely. It is a beautiful example of how a very simple random process can solve a non-trivial graph problem.

Las Vegas versus Monte Carlo: Las Vegas: correct always, time random. Monte Carlo: time fixed, correctness probabilistic. You can turn Las Vegas into Monte Carlo by stopping after a time limit and giving up or guessing. You can turn Monte Carlo into Las Vegas if you can quickly verify an answer: repeat until the verifier accepts. A memory trick: Las Vegas casinos never let you leave with the wrong amount of money, but you do not know how long you will stay.

Course cheat-sheet, analysis tools: Asymptotic notation O, Omega, Theta (lesson 2). Loop counting and invariants (lesson 3). Recurrences by substitution, unrolling, recursion trees and the master theorem (lessons 4 and 5). Amortized analysis by aggregate, accounting and potential (lesson 11). Lower bounds by decision trees (lesson 9). Reductions and NP-completeness (lesson 25).

Course cheat-sheet, design paradigms: Divide and conquer: split, solve, combine; merge sort, quick sort, Karatsuba, Strassen, closest pair. Greedy: one safe local choice, proved by exchange; activity selection, Huffman, Kruskal, Prim, Dijkstra. Dynamic programming: overlapping subproblems in a table; knapsack, LCS, edit distance, matrix chain, Floyd-Warshall, Bellman-Ford. Graph search: BFS, DFS, topological sort, SCC, max flow. Backtracking and branch and bound for exact search. Approximation and randomization for hard or huge problems.

Choosing a paradigm, a quick guide: If the problem splits into independent parts, try divide and conquer. If a simple rule seems to work and you can prove it with an exchange argument, use greedy. If brute force repeats the same subproblems, use DP. If it is about connections, model it as a graph. If it looks NP-hard, consider backtracking for small inputs and approximation or heuristics for large ones. Always start with a correct brute force and improve it.

Real life example 1, placing CCTV cameras: A city corporation wants cameras at intersections so that every street is watched. This is vertex cover. With thousands of intersections, an exact solution is too slow, but the 2-approximation runs in milliseconds and guarantees no more than twice the minimum number of cameras. Engineers then improve it locally, removing cameras that are not needed.

Real life example 2, secure messaging: When you set up a secure chat or log in to online banking, the server and your phone may need large random primes, for example to create RSA keys. They use the Miller-Rabin Monte Carlo test, repeated enough times that an error is less likely than a hardware fault. Randomization makes this fast and practically certain.

What to learn next: After this course, good next steps are Theory of Computation (automata, computability, complexity in depth), Advanced Algorithms (randomized and approximation algorithms, network flows, linear programming), Computational Geometry, and Machine Learning, which relies heavily on optimisation. For practice, solve problems on online judges like Codeforces, LeetCode or the Bangladeshi platform Toph, and take part in ICPC-style contests, where Bangladeshi university teams have a strong tradition.

Common mistakes and exam focus: Confusing approximation ratio direction for minimisation and maximisation; forgetting to state the lower bound in a ratio proof; mixing up Las Vegas and Monte Carlo; claiming randomized quick sort is Monte Carlo. Exams ask: 'Give a 2-approximation for vertex cover and prove the ratio.' 'Explain the MST-based approximation for metric TSP.' 'Differentiate Las Vegas and Monte Carlo with examples.' 'Which paradigm would you use for this problem and why?'

Recap: Approximation algorithms give provable closeness to optimal in polynomial time: vertex cover via a maximal matching is a 2-approximation; metric TSP via MST walk and shortcuts is a 2-approximation. Randomized algorithms use coin flips: Las Vegas is always correct with random time (randomized quick sort), Monte Carlo has fixed time with small error (Miller-Rabin, Freivalds). Across the course you learned to analyse algorithms and to design them with divide and conquer, greedy, DP, graph methods, search and approximation. Congratulations on finishing Algorithms.
key_points: An approximation algorithm runs in polynomial time with a proven ratio: C <= rho C* for minimisation.
Vertex cover 2-approximation: repeatedly take both ends of an uncovered edge; picked edges form a matching, so C* >= |A|.
Metric TSP 2-approximation: MST, full walk (2 w(T)), shortcut; w(T) <= C*. Christofides achieves 1.5.
Las Vegas: always correct, random time (randomized quick sort, quickselect).
Monte Carlo: fixed time, small error probability (Miller-Rabin, Freivalds); repeat to shrink error.
Paradigms: divide and conquer, greedy, DP, graph search, backtracking/branch and bound, approximation, randomization.
Next: Theory of Computation, Advanced Algorithms, and regular practice on online judges and contests.
lessons.tip: Make your own one-page cheat-sheet of every algorithm in this course with its paradigm, recurrence or key idea, and running time. Writing it yourself is the best revision before the final exam.
lessons.task: Draw a small map of 6 to 8 intersections near your home with streets as edges. Run the 2-approximation vertex cover by hand to place 'cameras', then try to find the true minimum by inspection and compare the two sizes.
